slides.title: Computer Basics and File Management
slides.content:
1. Objective: Learn to use computers for daily tasks.
  2. Today: Understand computers and organize files.
  3. Why It Matters: Save time writing, budgeting, and more!
  4. What do you want to do with a computer? (e.g., write a letter)
    5. Activity: Share one thing you want to do with a computer.
Step-by-step layer

Let us turn your wish into a clear goal.

  1. Take a pen and paper. Write one thing you want to do with a computer, for example "type a CV" or "track shop sales".
  2. Next to it, write the program that does it. Letters and CVs use Word. Numbers and budgets use Excel. Messages use email. Searching uses a browser.
  3. Make the goal small and exact: "Type a one-page letter to my landlord" is better than "learn Word".
  4. Share it with the class and keep the paper safe.

When it works, you have one to three goals, each linked to a program. If you feel stuck, think of something you now do on paper, such as writing a list or adding up money.

Power-user layer

Confident computer users always start with a goal, not with buttons. Ask: what do I want at the end, and which tool is best for it? Keep a simple "skills list" and tick each skill when you can do it without help.

  • Practise a little every day. Fifteen minutes daily beats three hours once a week.
  • Do real tasks: your own CV, your own budget.
  • Do not fear mistakes. Almost everything on a computer can be undone with Ctrl+Z.
  • Write down what you learn in your own words.
Check yourself: Name one thing you want to do on a computer and the program you would use for it.

Answer: Any real task with a matching program works, for example: type a letter in Word, or add monthly expenses in Excel.

slides.title: What Is a Computer?
slides.content:
1. A tool to create, store, and share information.
  2. Examples: Write letters, track expenses, browse the internet.
  3. Types: Desktop, laptop, tablet.
    4. Activity: Find and name the parts of a real computer.
Step-by-step layer

A computer takes in information, works on it, stores it and shows you the result. Try this on a real machine.

  1. Look at the computer in front of you. Is it a desktop (separate screen and box), a laptop (all in one, folds shut) or a tablet (touch screen)?
  2. Point to the screen, the keyboard and the mouse or touchpad.
  3. Find the power button and any USB ports (small slots for flash disks).
  4. Say out loud one thing this computer could do for you: create (a letter), store (photos), share (an email).

You are done when you can name the type and at least three parts. If you mix up laptop and tablet, remember: a laptop has a real keyboard attached.

Power-user layer

Think of a computer as four jobs: input (keyboard, mouse), processing (the CPU), storage (the drive) and output (screen, printer). When something fails, ask which job has the problem. No keys working is an input problem. A blank screen may be an output problem.

  • Memory (RAM) is the short-term workspace. Storage is the long-term cupboard.
  • Unsaved work lives only in memory, so save often.
  • Keep drinks away from keyboards and laptops.
Check yourself: Is a computer only for typing? Give two other things it does.

Answer: No. A computer creates, stores and shares information, so it can also keep records, do calculations, play media and browse the internet.

slides.title: Parts of a Computer
slides.content:
1. Monitor: Shows your work (like a TV).
  2. Keyboard: Type letters and numbers.
  3. Mouse: Click and move on the screen.
  4. CPU: The computer’s “brain.”
    5. Activity: Touch and use a keyboard and mouse.
Step-by-step layer

Learn to name each part by touching it.

  1. Find the monitor, the screen. Make sure it is switched on and that its cable is firmly plugged in.
  2. Place your hand on the keyboard. Find the letters, the number row and the large Spacebar.
  3. Hold the mouse lightly. Rest your index finger on the left button. On a laptop, use the touchpad instead.
  4. Find the CPU. On a desktop it is inside the box called the system unit. On a laptop it is inside the body.

It works when you can point to each part and say what it does. If the mouse does not move, check the cable or battery, or try another flat surface.

Power-user layer

Learn the other parts too. The RAM is short-term memory. The hard drive or SSD stores your files. The power supply feeds electricity. Printers and speakers are output devices.

  • Plug in cables gently. Never force a plug.
  • For a desktop, use a surge protector or UPS if power is unstable, so sudden cuts do not damage files.
  • Sit upright, with the screen at eye level and wrists relaxed.
Check yourself: Which part is the computer's brain, and which part shows your work?

Answer: The CPU is the brain. The monitor shows your work.

slides.title: Turning On/Off a Computer
slides.content:
1. Turn On: Press power button (icon: ⏻).
  2. Turn Off: Click “Start” → “Shut Down” (Windows).
  3. Wait until screen is off before leaving.
    4. Activity: Turn a computer on and off. Wait for it to shut down completely.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Check the computer is plugged in, or that the laptop is charged.
  2. Press the power button once (the ⏻ symbol). Do not hold it.
  3. Wait for the Windows sign-in screen. Type your PIN or password, then press Enter.
  4. To switch off, click Start (the Windows icon), then click the Power icon, then Shut down.
  5. Wait until the screen is completely dark and the lights stop.

It works when the desktop appears after sign-in, and the machine goes fully dark after shutdown. If the screen stays black after pressing power, check the plug and the monitor cable. If a program stops responding, wait a minute before doing anything harsh.

Power-user layer

Always save your work first, then close programs, then shut down. Never switch off by pulling the plug, because you can lose files or damage Windows.

  • Win+L locks the screen when you step away.
  • Use Restart when the computer is slow or after updates.
  • Use Sleep for short breaks, Shut down at the end of the day.
  • If everything is frozen, press and hold the power button only as a last resort.
Check yourself: Why should you use Start, Power, Shut down instead of just pulling the plug?

Answer: Windows needs time to close programs and save its settings. Pulling the plug can lose unsaved work and damage files.

slides.title: Using the Mouse
slides.content:
1. Left Click: Select items (e.g., open a folder).
  2. Right Click: Open options menu.
  3. Scroll: Move up/down a page.
  4. Drag: Move items by holding left click.
    5. Activity: Click and drag with the mouse. Play a simple game like Solitaire.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Hold the mouse with your palm on top. Put your index finger on the left button and middle finger on the right.
  2. Move the mouse slowly. Watch the pointer move on the screen.
  3. Click an icon once to select it. Double-click quickly to open it.
  4. Right-click an empty place on the desktop to see a menu. Press Esc to close it.
  5. Roll the wheel to scroll a page.
  6. Drag: press and hold the left button on an item, move, then release.

Open Solitaire to practise dragging cards. If the pointer reaches the edge of the table, lift the mouse and put it back. If double-click fails, click faster.

Power-user layer

You can do much without the mouse. Learn these and you will work faster.

KeysWhat it does
Ctrl+CCopy
Ctrl+VPaste
Ctrl+XCut
Ctrl+ZUndo

Avoid gripping the mouse hard. Rest your wrist. If you drag an item to the wrong place, press Ctrl+Z straight away.

Check yourself: What is the difference between a left click and a right click?

Answer: A left click selects or opens things. A right click opens a menu of options for whatever you clicked on.

slides.title: Exploring the Desktop
slides.content:
1. Desktop: Main screen with icons.
  2. Icons: Shortcuts to programs/files (e.g., File Explorer).
  3. Taskbar: Bottom bar to switch programs.
    4. Activity: Click an icon on a real desktop.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Look at the main screen after you sign in. This is the desktop.
  2. Find the icons, small pictures with names, such as Recycle Bin.
  3. Look at the bottom of the screen. The long bar is the taskbar. It has the Start button, a search box or icon, and icons of open or pinned programs.
  4. Double-click one desktop icon to open it. Click a taskbar icon to switch to that program.
  5. Look at the bottom-right for the clock and the Wi-Fi and sound icons.

It works when you can open an icon and move between two programs. If you open something by mistake, close it with the X at the top-right.

Power-user layer

Treat the desktop as a table top, not a storage room. Too many files on it make the computer slower to start and hard to search. Keep files in folders instead.

  • Win+D shows or hides the desktop.
  • Alt+Tab switches between open programs.
  • Right-click a program icon and choose Pin to taskbar for the programs you use daily.
  • Keep your desktop background plain so icons are easy to read.
Check yourself: What is the bar at the bottom of the screen called, and what is it used for?

Answer: It is the taskbar. It holds the Start button, search and icons so you can open and switch between programs.

slides.title: Opening File Explorer
slides.content:
1. File Explorer: Organizes documents, photos, etc.
  2. Open: Click File Explorer icon or search “File Explorer.”
  3. Shows folders like “Documents,” “Downloads.”
    4. Activity: Open File Explorer and look at folders.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Press the Windows key (the Windows logo key next to Ctrl and Alt), or click the Start button.
  2. Type File Explorer. Click it when it appears. Or click the yellow folder icon on the taskbar.
  3. Look at the left pane. You will see Home or Quick access, Desktop, Downloads, Documents, Pictures and This PC.
  4. Click Documents. The files inside appear on the right.
  5. Click Downloads and look at what is there.

It works when a window with folders opens. If it opens on a different view, click This PC on the left.

Power-user layer

Fast habit: press Win+E to open File Explorer instantly.

  • Alt+Left Arrow goes back. Alt+Up Arrow goes up one folder.
  • Click the address bar to see the full path of where you are.
  • Use the search box at the top-right to find a file by name.
  • Files you download go to Downloads. Move useful ones into proper folders, or you will lose track of them.
Check yourself: Name two ways to open File Explorer.

Answer: Click the folder icon on the taskbar, or press Start and type File Explorer. Pressing Win+E also works.

slides.title: Creating a Folder
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Open File Explorer.
  2. Step 2: Right-click → New → Folder.
  3. Step 3: Name it “My Files 2025.”
  4. Why? Keep letters, budgets organized.
    5. Activity: Create a folder named “My Files 2025.”
Step-by-step layer
  1. Open File Explorer and click Documents.
  2. Right-click on an empty white space in the window.
  3. Choose New, then Folder.
  4. The new folder appears with its name highlighted in blue. Type My Files 2025 and press Enter.

It works when you see a folder icon with your name under it. If you clicked away before naming it, right-click the folder, choose Rename (or select it and press F2), type the name and press Enter. If you right-clicked on a file instead of white space, the menu will be different. Press Esc and try again.

Power-user layer

Good folders save hours. Use clear, short names and do not put everything in one place.

  • Ctrl+Shift+N creates a new folder inside File Explorer.
  • Use one folder per topic or year, for example Letters, Budgets, CV.
  • Avoid names like "New folder (2)".
  • Do not use these characters in names: \ / : * ? " < > |.
  • Backup important folders on a flash disk or cloud storage regularly.
Check yourself: A folder you just made shows 'New folder'. How do you rename it?

Answer: Right-click it and choose Rename, or select it and press F2. Type the new name and press Enter.

slides.title: Saving a File
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Open a document (e.g., text file).
  2. Step 2: Click File → Save As.
  3. Step 3: Choose “My Files 2025” folder; name file (e.g., “Notes”).
    4. Activity: Save a text file in your new folder.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Open a program with a document, such as Notepad (search for it in Start).
  2. Type a few words.
  3. Click File then Save As. In Notepad, you can also press Ctrl+S for a new file.
  4. In the window, use the left side to go to Documents, then double-click My Files 2025.
  5. In the File name box type Notes.
  6. Click Save.

It works when the program's title bar shows Notes. Open the folder in File Explorer to see the file. If you cannot find it later, you probably saved it in a different folder. Search for its name.

Power-user layer

Save early, then save often. Pressing Ctrl+S every few minutes is the best habit you can build.

  • Use Save As to make a new copy under a different name, for example Notes v2.
  • Name files so you can understand them later: "Letter to Bank 2025", not "doc1".
  • Look at the file extension (such as .txt or .docx). It tells you what program opens it.
  • Keep a second copy of important files on a flash disk.
Check yourself: What is the difference between Save and Save As?

Answer: Save updates the file you already named. Save As lets you pick a new name or a new folder, making a new copy.

slides.title: Using the Calculator App
slides.content:
1. Open: Search “Calculator” in taskbar.
  2. Use for budgets, expenses.
  3. Example: $100 budget ÷ 5 items = $20/item.
    4. Activity: Calculate a sample expense (e.g., $50 ÷ 4).
Step-by-step layer
  1. Click Start or press the Windows key and type Calculator. Click it.
  2. Use the mouse to click the number buttons, or type on the keyboard. The number pad works best if Num Lock is on.
  3. For a sum such as 50 ÷ 4: type 50, press / (divide), type 4, press Enter.
  4. Read the answer on top: 12.5.
  5. Press Esc to clear, or click C.

On the keyboard, * means multiply and / means divide. If the answer looks wrong, check you typed the correct numbers and pressed the right sign.

Power-user layer

Calculators are quick but can mislead. Always do a rough check: 50 ÷ 4 should be a little more than 10, so 12.5 makes sense.

  • Use Ctrl+C to copy the answer and paste it elsewhere.
  • Recent versions have a history list so you can see earlier sums.
  • The menu in the top-left switches between Standard, Scientific and other modes.
  • For lists of numbers you will repeat or change, use Excel instead.
Check yourself: Use the Calculator to find 60 ÷ 3. What keys did you press?

Answer: The answer is 20. Press 60, then the divide key, then 3, then Enter or equals.

slides.title: Practical Activity
slides.content:
1. Task 1: Create a “My Files 2025” folder.
  2. Task 2: Save a text file (“Notes”) in the folder.
  3. Task 3: Calculate $60 ÷ 3 items.
    4. Activity: Complete each task and celebrate your progress!
Step-by-step layer

This is your first full practice. Take your time.

  1. Open File Explorer, then Documents. Right-click white space, choose New then Folder, name it My Files 2025.
  2. Open Notepad from Start. Type a short note about yourself.
  3. Click File then Save As. Choose My Files 2025. Name it Notes. Click Save.
  4. Open Calculator. Type 60, /, 3, Enter. Answer: 20.

Expected result: a Notes file inside the folder, and the answer 20. If the file is missing, search for Notes. Stretch: make a second folder inside it named Budgets, and find 450 ÷ 6 on Calculator.

Power-user layer

Check your work like a professional. Open File Explorer, open the folder and confirm the file is really there before you celebrate.

  • Repeat the whole task once without looking at the notes. This builds memory.
  • Try with the keyboard: Win+E, Ctrl+Shift+N, and Ctrl+S.
  • Write down any step that confused you and ask in the next class.
  • Teach someone else. Explaining is the quickest way to learn.
Check yourself: Where should the Notes file be when you finish the practical?

Answer: Inside the My Files 2025 folder, which is inside Documents.

slides.title: Why This Matters
slides.content:
1. Organize personal documents.
  2. Calculate expenses quickly.
  3. Prepare for typing next week!
    4. Activity: List one way these skills will help you in daily life.
Step-by-step layer

Computer skills are tools for earning and managing money. Think about where you could use today's skills.

  1. Write down three papers you handle now: for example, receipts, school fees records, CVs, price lists.
  2. Next to each, write how a folder or file could organize it.
  3. Write one number task you do by hand, such as splitting costs, and how Calculator can help.
  4. Share one example with the class.

You will see that folders keep important documents easy to find, and that calculators cut mistakes. Many jobs, small businesses and online applications now expect these basics. If you cannot think of an example, imagine running a small shop.

Power-user layer

Employers and customers notice people who are organized. Finding a document in seconds, instead of searching for ten minutes, shows professionalism.

  • Name files clearly, with dates when needed.
  • Keep one folder system, and use it every time.
  • Back up important documents, such as certificates and business records.
  • Practice a little daily. Skill grows from repetition.

Small habits today lead to confident, paid digital work tomorrow.

Check yourself: Give one way folders or the Calculator could help in a job or small business.

Answer: For example, folders keep invoices and customer letters easy to find, and the Calculator helps check totals quickly. Any realistic example is fine.

slides.title: Q&A and Homework
slides.content:
1. Ask: Any questions about today?
  2. Homework:
    1. Turn on/off computer 3 times.
    2. Create a folder and save a file.
    3. Calculate a simple expense.
  3. Next Week: Typing and creating documents!
    4. Activity: Choose one homework task and do it before the next class.
Step-by-step layer

Here are real beginner questions with short answers.

  • Will I break the computer if I click the wrong thing? Rarely. Most mistakes can be closed or undone with Ctrl+Z.
  • I saved a file but cannot find it. What now? Open File Explorer and type the file name in the search box at the top-right.
  • The mouse pointer will not move. Check the cable or battery, and clean the bottom of the mouse.
  • Do I have to shut down every time? Use Sleep for short breaks. Shut down at the end of the day.

Do the three homework tasks before next class.

Power-user layer

Good learners ask questions and keep notes. Write down a problem and what fixed it. That list becomes your own help guide.

  • When stuck, read the message on the screen slowly. It often tells you what to do.
  • Try again calmly, one change at a time.
  • Search the exact error message on the internet when you have access.
  • Repeat homework three times. The third time feels easy.
Check yourself: Your teacher says 'save your file in My Files 2025'. Where do you look to check that the file is there?

Answer: Open File Explorer, go to Documents, open the My Files 2025 folder and look for the file name.

slides.title: Typing and Document Creation
slides.content:
1. Objective: Learn to type and make documents.
  2. Today: Use Microsoft Word to write and save letters.
  3. Why It Matters: Create letters, lists, or notes easily!
  4. What kind of document would you like to write? (e.g., a letter to a friend)
Step-by-step layer

Choose your first document.

  1. Think of a short document you need: a letter, a to-do list, an invitation or a CV.
  2. Write its purpose in one line, for example "A letter asking my friend to visit".
  3. List who will read it. This tells you how formal to be.
  4. Write down three words to say in it.

Keep this plan. You will turn it into a real Word document by the end of the module. If you cannot decide, choose a letter, because it uses everything you will learn: typing, formatting and saving.

Power-user layer

Professionals plan before typing. They decide the purpose, the reader and the key points first, then write. This saves time and gives clearer documents.

  • Begin with the most important point.
  • Keep sentences short.
  • Check spelling before you share.
  • Save the file early with a clear name, and save again as you go with Ctrl+S.
Check yourself: Before you type a letter, which two things should you decide first?

Answer: Decide the purpose of the document and who will read it. Then list the main points.

slides.title: What Is Microsoft Word?
slides.content:
1. A program to type and format documents.
  2. Examples: Letters, to-do lists, invitations.
  3. Alternative: Google Docs (works in a browser).
⭐ Activity: Open Word or Google Docs on your computer.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Open Microsoft Word, or open Google Docs in a browser such as Chrome or Edge and sign in with a Google account.
  2. Choose Blank document.
  3. Look at the white page. This is where you type.
  4. At the top, find the ribbon, the strip of buttons with tabs such as Home and Insert.
  5. Look for Bold, written B, on the Home tab.

It works when you see a white page and a blinking line, called the cursor. If Word shows many templates, pick Blank document. LibreOffice Writer is a free alternative that works like Word and runs without internet.

Power-user layer

Word and Google Docs do similar jobs. Docs saves automatically online and is easy to share. Word is powerful, and works offline. Files made in Word end in .docx.

  • Ctrl+N starts a new blank document.
  • Use the search box on the ribbon to find a command (called Search or Tell Me in different versions).
  • Keep your files organized in folders.
  • Learn one tool well before many.
Check yourself: Name one free alternative to Microsoft Word.

Answer: Google Docs (in a browser) or LibreOffice Writer are free alternatives.

slides.title: Opening Microsoft Word
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Click Start (Windows icon, bottom-left).
  2. Step 2: Type “Word” in the search bar.
  3. Step 3: Click Microsoft Word to open.
⭐ Activity: Open Word on your own computer.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Click the Start button at the bottom-left, or press the Windows key.
  2. Type Word.
  3. Click Word in the results.
  4. If a start screen appears, click Blank document.
  5. Wait for the white page to appear.

It works when you see a white page with the ribbon on top. If Word is not found, check the spelling, or ask your teacher if it is installed. In some cases you may be asked to sign in with a Microsoft account. If you do not have one, ask your teacher or use LibreOffice or Google Docs instead.

Power-user layer

You can pin Word to the taskbar or Start for quick access: right-click its icon and choose Pin to taskbar.

  • Open Word faster: press the Windows key, type a few letters, press Enter.
  • Use Win+R, type winword and press Enter. It also opens Word on most machines.
  • Recent versions show recent files on the start screen. Click one to continue your work.
  • Close extra windows you are not using.
Check yourself: What do you type in the Start search box to find Word?

Answer: Type Word, then click Microsoft Word in the results.

slides.title: Understanding the Keyboard
slides.content:
1. Letters: Type words (e.g., A, B, C).
  2. Numbers: At the top or number pad.
  3. Spacebar: Add spaces between words.
  4. Enter: Start a new line.
  5. Backspace: Delete mistakes.
⭐ Activity: Touch the keys on a real keyboard.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Look at your keyboard. Find the letter keys in the middle. The number row is above them.
  2. Open Word and click on the white page.
  3. Press Spacebar and type a word. Add a space between words.
  4. Press Enter to start a new line.
  5. Type a wrong letter on purpose, then press Backspace to delete it.
  6. Hold Shift and press a letter for a capital.

You are done when you can type "Hello" and fix a mistake. If you get numbers instead of letters or the other way round, check Caps Lock and Num Lock.

Power-user layer

Touch typing means typing without looking at the keys. Rest your fingers on the home row: A S D F and J K L ;. Feel the small bumps on F and J.

  • Practise slowly and accurately first. Speed comes later.
  • Shift gives capitals. Caps Lock keeps them on.
  • Delete removes the letter in front of the cursor. Backspace removes the one behind.
  • Sit upright and take short breaks.
Check yourself: Which key deletes a mistake you just typed, and which key starts a new line?

Answer: Backspace deletes the mistake, and Enter starts a new line.

slides.title: Typing Your First Words
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Open Word (blank document).
  2. Step 2: Click in the white area.
  3. Step 3: Type a sentence (e.g., “Hello, my name is [Your Name]”).
  4. Use Backspace to fix mistakes.
⭐ Activity: Type your name.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Open Word and choose Blank document.
  2. Click once on the white page. A blinking line (the cursor) shows where typing will appear.
  3. Type Hello, my name is and then your name.
  4. Press Backspace if you make a mistake and retype.
  5. Press Enter to start a new line, then type another sentence.

Word may underline words in red (possible spelling error) or blue (possible grammar issue). Right-click the underlined word to see suggestions. If your typing appears in the wrong place, click where you want it to go. If letters overwrite others, press the Insert key.

Power-user layer

Do not press Enter at the end of every line. Word wraps text by itself. Press Enter only to begin a new paragraph.

  • Ctrl+Z undoes your last action. Ctrl+Y redoes it.
  • Use Home and End to jump to the start or end of a line.
  • Read what you typed before saving.
  • Use proper capitals for names and the start of sentences.
Check yourself: What does a red wavy line under a word usually mean in Word?

Answer: It usually means a possible spelling mistake. Right-click it to see suggested corrections.

slides.title: Saving Your Document
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Click File → Save As.
  2. Step 2: Choose “My Files 2025” folder (from Week 1).
  3. Step 3: Name file (e.g., “My Letter”).
  4. Step 4: Click Save.
⭐ Activity: Save your document in the Module 1 folder.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Click File at the top-left.
  2. Click Save As. In recent versions, then click Browse or This PC.
  3. Go to Documents and open My Files 2025.
  4. In File name, type My Letter.
  5. Click Save.

It works when the title at the top of Word now says My Letter. If your version offers OneDrive, you can choose it, but always check the folder shown. If you cannot find your file later, search for its name in File Explorer. You may also see a file type such as Word Document (.docx). Keep that.

Power-user layer

The first time you save, name the file. After that, press Ctrl+S often. In Microsoft 365, if a file is saved on OneDrive, AutoSave may keep saving for you, but do not depend on it.

  • F12 opens Save As.
  • Use clear names with dates for versions: Letter 2025-03.
  • Do not save on a computer that others share, unless it is your own folder.
  • Keep a backup copy of important files.
Check yourself: After your first save, which shortcut updates the file quickly?

Answer: Press Ctrl+S.

slides.title: Formatting Text
slides.content:
1. Bold: Highlight text, click Bold (B icon).
  2. Font Size: Change size (e.g., 14pt for body, 16pt for titles).
  3. Alignment: Center text (e.g., for a title).
⭐ Activity: Use the formatting toolbar to change text style and color.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Type a word or sentence. Select it by dragging over it with the mouse, until it is highlighted.
  2. Click the Home tab.
  3. Click B for bold.
  4. Click the Font Size box and choose a size, for example 16.
  5. Click the Center button to center the text.
  6. Click the arrow next to the Font Color button (the letter A with a coloured line) and choose a colour.

It works when your text changes. If nothing changes, the text was not selected. Select it again. To remove formatting, press Ctrl+Z.

Power-user layer

Use formatting to help the reader, not to decorate. Use one or two fonts and simple colours.

KeysAction
Ctrl+BBold
Ctrl+IItalic
Ctrl+UUnderline
Ctrl+ECenter
Ctrl+ASelect all

Select first, then format. Body text around 11 or 12 points is easy to read.

Check yourself: What must you do to text before you can make it bold?

Answer: You must select (highlight) it first, then click Bold or press Ctrl+B.

slides.title: Creating a Letter
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Type a title (e.g., “Dear Friend”).
  2. Step 2: Press Enter for a new line.
  3. Step 3: Type 2-3 sentences (e.g., “I hope you’re well. Let’s meet soon.”).
  4. Step 4: Format title (Bold, Center, 16pt).
✉️ Guide: Help learners type and format a short letter.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Open a blank document. Type Dear Friend, and press Enter.
  2. Type two or three sentences, for example: I hope you are well. Let us meet soon.
  3. Press Enter and type Yours sincerely, then Enter and your name.
  4. Select the first line. On the Home tab, click Bold, Center, and set size 16.
  5. Save it as My Letter.

It works when the top line looks bigger and centered. If the whole letter changed, you selected too much. Press Ctrl+Z and select only the top line. Letters usually include the date and a greeting, so add them if you can.

Power-user layer

A good letter is short and clear: greeting, reason for writing, details, polite ending. In a formal letter, include the date and the receiver's address.

  • Use Ctrl+E to center a title and Ctrl+L to return to left alignment.
  • Leave a blank line between paragraphs.
  • Check names and spelling. Read it aloud.
  • Save a copy as a template, so you can reuse the layout.
Check yourself: Which line of your letter was formatted bold, centered and 16 pt?

Answer: The title line (for example, Dear Friend). Bold, Center and size 16 were applied to it.

slides.title: Using Bullets for Lists
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Click the Bullets icon in Word.
  2. Step 2: Type items (e.g., “Buy groceries,” “Call friend”).
  3. Step 3: Press Enter to add more items.
📝 Activity: Learners create a to-do list.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Click on a new line in Word.
  2. On the Home tab, click the Bullets button (a list with dots).
  3. Type your first item, for example Buy groceries, and press Enter.
  4. A new bullet appears. Type Call friend, press Enter, then a third item.
  5. To finish the list, press Enter on an empty bullet, or press Enter twice.

It works when each item has a dot at the start. If the dots disappear, click the Bullets button again. Use the Numbering button next to it when order matters, such as steps.

Power-user layer

Lists are easier to read than long paragraphs. Keep each item short and start them the same way, for example with a verb.

  • Ctrl+Shift+L turns bullets on or off.
  • Press Tab at the start of a bullet to make a sub-point.
  • Use numbers for steps, bullets when order does not matter.
  • Do not make a bullet list too long. Break into groups.
Check yourself: When would you choose a numbered list instead of bullets?

Answer: When the order matters, such as steps in a process.

slides.title: Saving and Closing
slides.content:
1. Save: Click File → Save (or Ctrl+S) to update.
  2. Close: Click File → Close or the red X (top-right).
  3. Reopen: Open File Explorer, find “My Files 2025,” double-click file.
⭐ Activity: Save and reopen your file.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Press Ctrl+S to save. Or click File then Save.
  2. Close the document: click File then Close, or click the X at the top-right. This may close Word as well.
  3. If Word asks "Do you want to save changes?", click Save.
  4. Open File Explorer, go to Documents, then My Files 2025.
  5. Double-click your file to reopen it.

It works when your text appears again. If you cannot see the file, check the folder. Also look at File then Open, or Recent in Word. Never click Don't Save unless you want to lose your changes.

Power-user layer

The red X closes the window. The Save dialog is your safety net. Read it carefully.

  • Save before closing and again before printing or emailing.
  • Word can recover some unsaved work after a crash, but never rely on it.
  • Ctrl+W closes the current document. Alt+F4 closes the window.
  • Use File then Open and the Recent list to reopen files quickly.
Check yourself: Word asks 'Do you want to save changes?' when you close. What should you click if you want to keep your work?

Answer: Click Save.

slides.title: Practical Activity
slides.content:
1. Task 1: Open Word and type a short letter (3 sentences).
  2. Task 2: Format the title (Bold, Center, 16pt).
  3. Task 3: Save the letter as “My Letter” in “My Files 2025.”
  4. Task 4: Create a bulleted to-do list (3 items).
✅ Checklist: Complete each task and celebrate progress!
Step-by-step layer

Complete these tasks in order.

  1. Open Word and choose Blank document.
  2. Type Dear Friend, then Enter. Type three sentences.
  3. Select the title line. On Home, click Bold, Center and set size 16.
  4. Press Enter twice. Click Bullets and type three to-do items.
  5. Press Ctrl+S, go to Documents, My Files 2025, name it My Letter, and click Save.

Expected result: a letter with a big centered title, three sentences and a bullet list, saved in the folder. Stretch: add a closing line and your name, make the closing italic, and save a copy named My Letter 2.

Power-user layer

When you finish, reopen the file to prove it was saved properly. Close it, find it in File Explorer and double-click.

  • Check spelling: red lines mean look again.
  • Use shortcuts: Ctrl+B, Ctrl+E, Ctrl+Shift+L, Ctrl+S.
  • Print preview shows how the page will look: File then Print.
  • Keep the file as a template for future letters.
Check yourself: After the practical, how can you prove your letter was really saved?

Answer: Close Word, open File Explorer, open My Files 2025 and double-click My Letter. The letter should open with your text.

slides.title: Why This Matters
slides.content:
1. Write letters to friends or family.
  2. Create lists for planning or tasks.
  3. Prepare for spreadsheets next week!
⏳ Note: These skills help in daily life.
Step-by-step layer

Word skills open doors to real tasks.

  1. List three documents people need: a CV, a business letter, a price list, a notice, an invitation.
  2. Choose one you could make for yourself or someone else.
  3. Write what it would help you achieve, for example applying for a job or quoting a customer.

A tidy CV or letter can make a good first impression on an employer. Small businesses need quotations, receipts and notices, and many people pay for neat typing and printing. These skills also lead into email and office work. If you cannot think of an example, imagine writing a notice for your church, shop or school.

Power-user layer

The people who get paid for document work are the ones who are accurate and neat. Learn to proofread, format consistently and meet deadlines.

  • Create a CV template you can update.
  • Save a PDF copy when sending documents (File then Save As, choose PDF in the type list).
  • Keep client files in separate folders.
  • Build a small portfolio of your best work.
Check yourself: Name one real task where Word could help you earn or save money.

Answer: For example, typing a CV for a job application, or preparing quotations for customers.

slides.title: Q&A and Homework
slides.content:
1. Ask: Any questions about typing or Word?
  2. Homework:
    1. Type a 3-sentence letter and save it.
    2. Create a bulleted list of 3 tasks.
    3. Reopen your saved letter.
  3. Next Week: Spreadsheets for organizing numbers!
❓ Encourage: Ask questions and use handouts for practice.
Step-by-step layer

Common beginner questions about typing and Word.

  • Why are my letters all capitals? Caps Lock is on. Press it once to switch off.
  • I made a mistake. Can I undo it? Yes. Press Ctrl+Z.
  • I closed Word without saving. Is my work gone? Maybe. Reopen Word and look under File then Open, Recent, or recover unsaved documents. Save early next time.
  • How can I type faster? Practise a few minutes daily, look at the screen and use all fingers.

Homework: type a three-sentence letter, make a three-item bullet list and reopen your saved letter.

Power-user layer

Keep practising. Free online typing practice sites exist, so check what is currently available. Even ten minutes a day helps.

  • Use handouts to repeat the steps.
  • Always save with Ctrl+S as you go.
  • Do the homework on a real computer, not just in your head.
  • Write questions down as they come, and ask them in class.
Check yourself: You type in all capitals by accident. Which key do you press?

Answer: Press Caps Lock to turn it off.

slides.title: Introduction to Spreadsheets
slides.content:
1. Objective: Learn to organize numbers and lists.
  2. Today: Use Excel to track expenses and calculate totals.
  3. Why It Matters: Manage budgets or plans easily!
  4. What would you like to track? (e.g., grocery expenses)
Step-by-step layer

Decide what you will track.

  1. Think of something with numbers: grocery spending, school fees, shop sales, savings.
  2. Write down the columns you would need, for example Date, Item, Cost.
  3. Think of the question you want answered, such as "How much did I spend this month?"
  4. Share your idea with the class.

It works when you have a topic, two or three column names and one question. If you cannot decide, track your weekly spending on food. That gives you something real to practise with, and it needs addition, which is the first thing a spreadsheet does.

Power-user layer

Experts design the question first. A spreadsheet works best when you know what answer you need before you enter numbers.

  • One row for each record, one column for each type of information.
  • Put headings in the first row.
  • Keep the data tidy. Do not leave random blank rows.
  • Save early, and back up your file.
Check yourself: What is the first question to ask before building a spreadsheet?

Answer: What do I want to find out or track? That tells you which columns you need.

slides.title: What Is Microsoft Excel?
slides.content:
1. A program to organize numbers and lists in tables.
  2. Examples: Budgets, event plans, shopping lists.
  3. Alternative: Google Sheets (works in a browser).
⭐ Activity: Open Excel or Google Sheets on your computer.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Open Excel from Start, or open Google Sheets in your browser.
  2. Choose Blank workbook.
  3. You will see a grid of boxes. Each box is a cell.
  4. Click a cell and type your name. Press Enter.
  5. Look at the tabs at the bottom, such as Sheet1. This is one sheet in a workbook.

It works when you see a grid with letters across the top and numbers down the side. Excel files end in .xlsx. If you opened the wrong program, close it and try again. LibreOffice Calc is a free alternative that works similarly.

Power-user layer

Excel is for storing, calculating and analysing data. Use Word for text and Excel for numbers. A workbook can have many sheets, so you can keep one for each month.

  • Do not type numbers in Word if you need to add them.
  • Use Ctrl+N for a new workbook.
  • Name your sheet tabs by double-clicking them.
  • Google Sheets makes it easy to share and edit with others at the same time.
Check yourself: When would you use Excel instead of Word?

Answer: When you need to organize numbers or lists in a table and calculate with them, such as budgets or totals.

slides.title: Opening Microsoft Excel
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Click Start (Windows icon, bottom-left).
  2. Step 2: Type “Excel” in the search bar.
  3. Step 3: Click Microsoft Excel to open.
⭐ Activity: Open Excel on your own computer.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Click the Start button or press the Windows key.
  2. Type Excel.
  3. Click Excel in the results.
  4. On the start screen, click Blank workbook.
  5. Wait for the grid to appear.

It works when you see rows, columns and the ribbon. If Excel is not found, check the spelling or ask whether it is installed. Excel may ask you to sign in. If you cannot, use Google Sheets or LibreOffice Calc instead. If a message says the file is in Protected View, click Enable Editing only when you trust the file.

Power-user layer

Pin Excel to the taskbar for faster access. Recent versions of Excel show templates for budgets and planners, but start with a blank workbook to learn the basics.

  • Type a few letters after pressing the Windows key, then press Enter.
  • Use Ctrl+O to open a saved file.
  • Keep only the workbooks you need open.
  • Save a new workbook straight away.
Check yourself: After you click Start and type Excel, what do you click on the start screen to begin?

Answer: Blank workbook.

slides.title: Understanding Spreadsheets
slides.content:
1. Cells: Boxes where you type data (e.g., A1, B2).
  2. Rows: Horizontal lines (numbered 1, 2, 3...).
  3. Columns: Vertical lines (lettered A, B, C...).
  4. Example: Type “Groceries” in cell A1.
⭐ Activity: Find and name cells, rows, and columns in a spreadsheet.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Open Excel with a blank workbook.
  2. Look across the top: the letters A, B, C are columns. Look down the left: the numbers 1, 2, 3 are rows.
  3. Click the cell where column A meets row 1. This is A1. Look at the Name Box on the left above the grid. It shows A1.
  4. Type Groceries and press Enter.
  5. Click cell B2 (column B, row 2) and check the Name Box.

It works when the Name Box matches the cell you clicked. Always read the column letter first, then the row number. If you mix them, remember: letters go across, numbers go down.

Power-user layer

The cell address is how formulas find numbers, so learn to read them quickly. A range such as B1:B5 means from B1 down to B5.

  • Ctrl+Home goes to A1.
  • Ctrl+Arrow jumps to the end of a block of data.
  • Click a column letter to select the whole column, or a row number to select the whole row.
  • Click the Name Box and type a cell such as D10, then press Enter, to jump there.
Check yourself: What is the address of the cell in column C, row 4?

Answer: C4. The column letter comes first, then the row number.

slides.title: Entering Data
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Click a cell (e.g., A1).
  2. Step 2: Type data (e.g., “Milk” or “$5”).
  3. Step 3: Press Enter to move to the next cell.
  4. Tip: Use arrow keys to move between cells.
⭐ Activity: Type a simple list in Excel.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Click cell A1. Type Milk and press Enter. The cursor moves down to A2.
  2. Type Bread and press Enter.
  3. Click B1. Type 5 and press Enter. Type 3 in B2.
  4. Use the arrow keys to move between cells without clicking.
  5. To change an entry, click the cell and type again, or press F2 to edit what is there.

It works when your words sit on the left and numbers on the right of their cells. If text is cut off, do not worry, the full text is still there. If you type a number as text, such as 5 shillings, Excel cannot add it. Type only the number.

Power-user layer

Type plain numbers and let formatting add currency signs. Typing "KSh 500" as text can stop calculations from working. Select the cells and use the Number Format options on the Home tab.

  • Tab moves right. Enter moves down. Shift+Enter moves up.
  • Esc cancels what you are typing.
  • Delete clears the selected cells.
  • Check typing, because one wrong digit changes the total.
Check yourself: Why is it better to type 500 instead of 500 shillings in a cost cell?

Answer: Excel can add only numbers. Text such as '500 shillings' is treated as words and cannot be calculated.

slides.title: Saving Your Spreadsheet
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Click File → Save As.
  2. Step 2: Choose “My Files 2025” folder (from Week 1).
  3. Step 3: Name file (e.g., “My Budget”).
  4. Step 4: Click Save.
⭐ Activity: Save your spreadsheet in the Module 3 folder.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Click File then Save As. In recent versions, click Browse or This PC.
  2. Go to Documents and open My Files 2025.
  3. In File name, type My Budget.
  4. Check the type says Excel Workbook.
  5. Click Save.

It works when the title bar at the top shows My Budget. Later, press Ctrl+S to update the same file. If you cannot find the file, search for My Budget in File Explorer. If you are asked about saving in a different format, choose to keep the Excel format unless you were told otherwise.

Power-user layer

Spreadsheets hold important numbers, so save often. Ctrl+S after every few entries is a good habit. F12 opens Save As.

  • Use clear names with the month or year: Budget March.
  • Before big changes, Save As a copy so you can go back.
  • If your file is on OneDrive, AutoSave may be on. Still press Save before closing.
  • Keep backups of business files.
Check yourself: After the first save, what is the quick way to save changes again?

Answer: Press Ctrl+S.

slides.title: Basic Formatting
slides.content:
1. Bold: Highlight cell, click Bold (B icon).
  2. Borders: Add lines around cells (Border icon).
  3. Column Width: Drag column edges to fit text.
⭐ Activity: Format and adjust columns in your spreadsheet.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Type headings in A1 and B1, then some data below.
  2. Select the heading row: click cell A1, hold the mouse and drag to B1.
  3. On the Home tab, click B for bold.
  4. Select the cells with data. Click the Borders button (a small square grid icon) and choose All Borders.
  5. Move the mouse to the line between the column letters A and B. When it becomes a double arrow, drag to widen. Or double-click the line to fit automatically.

It works when headings are bold, cells have lines and text fits. If you see ##### in a cell, the column is too narrow for the number. Widen it.

Power-user layer

Clean formatting makes a spreadsheet look professional and easier to read. Keep it simple: bold headings, borders, enough width.

  • Ctrl+B makes bold.
  • Ctrl+1 opens Format Cells, where you set number style, such as currency.
  • Select columns and double-click a border to auto-fit.
  • Use Ctrl+Z if a format goes wrong.
  • Avoid too many colours.
Check yourself: A cell shows ##### instead of your number. What is the usual fix?

Answer: The column is too narrow. Widen it by dragging its edge or double-clicking the border.

slides.title: Simple Calculations (SUM)
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Type numbers (e.g., $5, $10, $15 in B1:B3).
  2. Step 2: Click a cell for the total (e.g., B4).
  3. Step 3: Type =SUM(B1:B3) and press Enter.
  4. Example: $5 + $10 + $15 = $30.
⭐ Activity: Calculate a total using the SUM formula.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Type 5 in B1, 10 in B2 and 15 in B3.
  2. Click cell B4.
  3. Type =SUM(B1:B3). Begin with the equals sign.
  4. Press Enter.
  5. B4 shows 30.

B1:B3 means "from B1 to B3". Click B4 again and look at the formula bar above the grid to see the formula. If you see the formula text instead of the answer, you may have typed a space or apostrophe before the equals sign. If you see an error such as #NAME?, check the spelling of SUM. Also try the quick way: select B4 and press Alt+=.

Power-user layer

A formula updates by itself when the numbers change. That is the power of Excel. Change B2 to 20 and the total changes at once.

  • Alt+= inserts AutoSum quickly.
  • Click cells instead of typing addresses while writing a formula.
  • Every formula starts with =.
  • Do not type the total yourself. Always use a formula.
  • Check the range covers all your numbers.
Check yourself: What does the formula =SUM(B1:B3) do?

Answer: It adds the numbers in cells B1, B2 and B3 and shows the total.

slides.title: Creating an Expense Tracker
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Label A1: “Item,” B1: “Cost.”
  2. Step 2: Enter items (e.g., “Milk,” “Bread” in A2:A3).
  3. Step 3: Enter costs (e.g., $2, $3 in B2:B3).
  4. Step 4: Use SUM in B4 to calculate total.
📋 Guide: Help learners build a tracker.
Step-by-step layer
  1. In A1 type Item. In B1 type Cost.
  2. In A2 type Milk, in A3 type Bread.
  3. In B2 type 2, in B3 type 3.
  4. In A4 type Total. In B4 type =SUM(B2:B3) and press Enter.
  5. Make A1 and B1 bold, and add borders.

It works when B4 shows 5. If you add a new item below row 3, the total will not include it unless the range is extended. Change the formula to cover the new row. Adding the new row above the total row usually extends the SUM automatically in recent versions, but always check the formula.

Power-user layer

Add a Date column and you have a real tracker. Leave room for new items by keeping the total at the top or on a different sheet.

  • Select a whole data range and use Insert then Table (or Ctrl+T) so formulas grow with your data.
  • Use clear headings, one item per row.
  • Format costs with the currency option.
  • Check your total against a calculator once.
Check yourself: Why must the SUM range include every cost row?

Answer: The formula only adds what is inside its range. If a row is outside the range, it will be left out of the total.

slides.title: Checking Your Work
slides.content:
1. Check: Are numbers correct? Is text clear?
  2. Save: Click File → Save (or Ctrl+S).
  3. Reopen: Open File Explorer, find “My Files 2025,” double-click file.
⭐ Activity: Save and reopen your file.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Look at every number. Compare it with your paper list or receipt.
  2. Click the total cell and check that the formula covers all the cells.
  3. Check headings and spelling. Make sure words are clear.
  4. Press Ctrl+S to save.
  5. Close Excel. Open File Explorer, then Documents, then My Files 2025. Double-click the file to reopen it.

It works when your numbers and total appear again exactly as before. If a total looks wrong, click it and read the formula. A wrong total is usually a typing error or a range that is too short. If there is a green triangle in a cell corner, point at it to see Excel's warning.

Power-user layer

Always double-check numbers that matter. Professionals use a second method, such as adding on a calculator, or estimating roughly in their head.

  • Click on a cell to see its formula in the formula bar.
  • Look for text that looks like a number but is on the left of a cell.
  • Keep a copy before making big changes.
  • Save before closing, every time.
Check yourself: Your total looks too small. What is the first thing to check?

Answer: Check the formula's range, and make sure every cost was typed as a number, not text.

slides.title: Practical Activity
slides.content:
1. Task 1: Open Excel and create an expense tracker.
  2. Task 2: Enter 3 items and costs (e.g., “Milk,” $2).
  3. Task 3: Use SUM to calculate total cost.
  4. Task 4: Save as “My Budget” in “My Files 2025.”
✅ Checklist: Complete each task and celebrate progress!
Step-by-step layer

Build and save your first budget.

  1. Open Excel and choose Blank workbook.
  2. Type Item in A1 and Cost in B1.
  3. Enter three items in A2 to A4 and their costs in B2 to B4, for example Milk 2, Bread 3, Sugar 4.
  4. In A5 type Total. In B5 type =SUM(B2:B4), press Enter.
  5. Make row 1 bold. Add borders.
  6. Press Ctrl+S and save as My Budget in My Files 2025.

Expected result: total 9. Stretch: add two more items, extend the formula, and check it.

Power-user layer

Test your tracker: change one cost and watch the total update. That proves the formula works.

  • Check each entry against your source.
  • Alt+= is a quick way to add a total.
  • Use Tab and Enter to move fast.
  • Save a second version before experimenting.
  • Write down one thing you would improve next time.
Check yourself: In your tracker, costs are 2, 3 and 4. What should the total show, and what if you change 3 to 6?

Answer: The total shows 9. After changing 3 to 6, it becomes 12, because the formula updates automatically.

slides.title: Why This Matters
slides.content:
1. Track expenses (e.g., groceries, bills).
  2. Organize lists (e.g., events, tasks).
  3. Prepare for email next week!
⏳ Note: Spreadsheets help in real life.
Step-by-step layer

Excel is one of the most useful office skills.

  1. Think of a task with numbers in your life or work: shop stock, school fees, savings group contributions.
  2. Imagine it as a table with columns and rows.
  3. Write which formula you would need, such as a total.

Shop owners can track daily sales and spending, savings groups can record contributions, and families can plan bills. Many office jobs, and small business tasks, include working with numbers. People who can use spreadsheets well are often valued because they save time and avoid mistakes. If you are unsure, start with a list of your own monthly expenses.

Power-user layer

Spreadsheet skills grow with practice. After SUM, learn averages, sorting, filtering and charts. These turn raw numbers into decisions.

  • Keep monthly records in the same layout.
  • Protect important files with backups.
  • Do not share files containing private information.
  • Learn one new feature every week.
Check yourself: Give one example of how a shop owner or a savings group could use Excel.

Answer: A shop owner could record daily sales and expenses and total them. A savings group could record each member's contributions and total them.

slides.title: Q&A and Homework
slides.content:
1. Ask: Any questions about Excel?
  2. Homework:
    1. Create an expense tracker with 5 items.
    2. Calculate the total using SUM.
    3. Save and reopen the file.
  3. Next Week: Sending emails!
❓ Encourage: Ask questions and use handouts for practice.
Step-by-step layer

Common beginner questions about Excel.

  • Why does my formula show as text? You may have left out the equals sign, or put a space before it.
  • What does ##### mean? The column is too narrow. Widen it.
  • Can I use Excel without internet? Yes, if it is installed. Google Sheets needs a connection unless set up offline.
  • Is Excel the same as Word? No. Excel is for numbers and tables, Word for writing.

Homework: build a five-item expense tracker, total it with SUM, then save, close and reopen it.

Power-user layer

Always check your answers. If a total does not make sense, click it and read the formula.

  • Practise with real numbers from your life.
  • Use Ctrl+S as you work.
  • Keep your homework file in My Files 2025.
  • When you are stuck, read any error message slowly. It often tells you what is wrong.
Check yourself: Your formula =SUM(B1:B3) shows as plain text. What is the likely cause?

Answer: The equals sign is missing or there is a space or apostrophe before it. Retype it starting with =.

slides.title: Email Setup and Communication
slides.content:
1. Objective: Learn to use email for communication.
  2. Today: Set up Gmail and send messages.
  3. Why It Matters: Stay in touch with friends or family!
  4. Who would you like to email? (e.g., a family member)
Step-by-step layer

This is your starting checklist for the module.

  1. Make sure the computer is online. Look at the Wi-Fi icon at the bottom-right of the taskbar.
  2. Open Google Chrome (or Microsoft Edge).
  3. Get a pen and a notebook. You will write your new email address and password in it.
  4. Choose one person you want to email. Ask them for their email address.
  5. Copy that address into your notebook, letter by letter, exactly as given.

You are ready when a browser is open and one email address is written down. Common slip: no internet. Click the Wi-Fi icon, choose your network, type the Wi-Fi password, then try again.

Power-user layer
  • An email address has three parts: a name, the @ sign, and the service, for example name@gmail.com. One wrong letter sends your message to the wrong person or nowhere.
  • Email is the key to many other services. Job applications, school forms and password resets all arrive by email.
  • Choose a sensible address for work. Use your name, not a nickname.
  • Check your inbox every day. People expect replies.
  • Never share your password, even with friends.
Check yourself: What are the parts of an email address, and which symbol separates them?

Answer: The name part (like yourname) and the service part (like gmail.com). The @ sign goes between them.

slides.title: What Is Email?
slides.content:
1. A way to send and receive messages online.
  2. Examples: Send a thank-you note, share a document.
  3. We’ll use Gmail, a free email service.
📧 Explain: Email is like a digital letter; show Gmail on a projector.
Step-by-step layer

Let us compare email to a paper letter.

  1. On paper, write four labels: To, From, Subject, Message.
  2. Match them to a letter: the name on the envelope is To, the sender is From, the topic is Subject, and the letter inside is the Message.
  3. Open Chrome, click the address bar, type gmail.com and press Enter.
  4. Look at the page. If you have no account yet, you will only see a sign-in box. That is fine.

You should see that email has the same parts as a letter, only faster. Common slip: thinking email needs a special program. It does not. A browser is enough.

Power-user layer
  • Use email for formal messages, documents and anything you may need as proof later. Messages stay saved and searchable.
  • Gmail, Outlook.com and Yahoo are free services. A business can also have its own address, such as name@yourcompany.co.ke.
  • Email is not a sealed letter. Anyone can forward what you write, so write only what you are happy to be shared.
  • One main address you check daily is better than many forgotten ones.
Check yourself: Name two things you can send by email besides typed words.

Answer: Attachments such as documents, photos or spreadsheets, and links to web pages.

slides.title: Opening Gmail
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Open Google Chrome (browser).
  2. Step 2: Type “gmail.com” in the address bar.
  3. Step 3: Press Enter to go to Gmail.
⭐ Activity: Open Gmail on your own computer.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Click the Chrome icon on the taskbar, or press the Windows key, type Chrome and press Enter.
  2. Click once in the long bar at the top (the address bar).
  3. Type gmail.com.
  4. Press Enter.

You should see either a sign-in box or your inbox if someone already signed in. Common slips:

  • The message "This site can't be reached" means a spelling error. Click the address bar, press Ctrl+A to select the text, and type it again.
  • Someone else's inbox appears. Click the round profile picture at the top-right and choose Sign out, then sign in as yourself.

Typing in the Google search box also works, but the address bar is the right habit.

Power-user layer
  • Ctrl+L jumps to the address bar. Type gmail.com and press Enter. No mouse needed.
  • Press Ctrl+D to bookmark Gmail so you can open it in one click.
  • Right-click the Gmail tab and choose Pin to keep it small and always open.
  • Typing the address yourself is safer than clicking a link someone sent. A link can lead to a fake page.
  • On a shared computer, open a private window with Ctrl+Shift+N and close it when done.
Check yourself: Why is it safer to type gmail.com yourself than to click a link in a message?

Answer: A link can lead to a fake page that steals your password. Typing the address takes you to the real site.

slides.title: Creating a Gmail Account
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Click “Create account” on Gmail.
  2. Step 2: Enter your name, birthday, and password.
  3. Step 3: Choose an email address (e.g., yourname@gmail.com).
  4. Step 4: Sign in with your email and password.
📝 Help: Assist learners to create accounts; write down passwords securely.
Step-by-step layer
  1. On the Gmail page, click Create account and choose For my personal use.
  2. Type your first and last name. Click Next.
  3. Enter your birthday and the other details asked. Click Next.
  4. Pick one of the suggested addresses, or choose to create your own. Use letters, numbers and full stops, with no spaces.
  5. Type a password, then type it again to confirm.
  6. Follow the last screens. Google may ask for a phone number to check you are real. This is normal.

You should land in an inbox with a welcome message. If the address is taken, add a number or another word. Write your address and password in your notebook straight away.

Power-user layer
  • Your address will go on your CV, so choose something plain like firstname.lastname.
  • A strong password is long. Join several unrelated words and add numbers, and never use your birthday or name.
  • Never reuse the same password on other websites.
  • Add a recovery phone number or email, and turn on 2-Step Verification in your Google Account security settings.
  • Never tell anyone a code Google sends you, even if they say they are from Google.
  • Keep your notebook somewhere private.
Check yourself: Give two ways to keep your new password safe.

Answer: Make it long and different from your other passwords, keep any written copy private, and never share it or any code sent to you.

slides.title: Understanding the Gmail Inbox
slides.content:
1. Inbox: Shows received emails.
  2. Compose: Button to write a new email.
  3. Sent: Shows emails you’ve sent.
⭐ Activity: Find and name the key areas in your Gmail inbox.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Sign in to Gmail.
  2. Look at the left side. You will see a Compose button, then a list: Inbox, Starred, Sent, Drafts and more. Click More to see the rest.
  3. Click Inbox. Messages you received appear here. Bold ones are not yet read.
  4. Click Sent to see messages you sent.
  5. At the top, find the Search mail box. At the top-right, find your round profile picture.
  6. Click a message to open it. Click the back arrow to return.

If the left list is hidden, click the three-line menu at the top-left. Tabs such as Promotions hold advertising mail.

Power-user layer
  • Search is powerful. Try from:john, has:attachment or is:unread.
  • Check the Spam folder now and then. Real mail is sometimes placed there.
  • Drafts keeps unfinished messages automatically.
  • Gmail keyboard shortcuts must be switched on first: Settings gear, See all settings, General, Keyboard shortcuts on. Then c composes and / goes to search.
  • Star important mail so you can find it fast.
Check yourself: Where do you look to find an email you already sent?

Answer: In the Sent folder, in the list on the left side of Gmail.

slides.title: Writing an Email
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Click “Compose” in Gmail.
  2. Step 2: Type recipient’s email in “To” field.
  3. Step 3: Add a subject (e.g., “Hello”).
  4. Step 4: Type a message (e.g., “Hi, hope you’re well!”).
  5. Step 5: Click “Send.”
⭐ Activity: Send an email to a classmate.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Click Compose. A new message window opens at the bottom-right.
  2. In To, type the address. Press Enter or Tab.
  3. Click Subject and type a short, clear subject.
  4. Click the large body area. Write a greeting, your message, thanks, and your name.
  5. Read it once and check the address.
  6. Click the blue Send button.

You should see "Message sent" at the bottom-left of the screen. Red underlines are spelling hints. Right-click the word to fix it. If a "Delivery incident" or "Address not found" message comes back, the address had a mistake. Send again with the right one.

Power-user layer
  • Ctrl+Enter sends the message. Tab moves between fields.
  • Cc shows other recipients to everyone. Bcc hides them. Use Bcc for groups so you protect people's addresses.
  • Write a subject that says what you need, such as "Meeting request: Friday 10am".
  • Type the To address last, so a half-written message cannot go out by accident.
  • After sending, an Undo link shows for a few seconds. Use it fast if you spot a mistake.
Check yourself: What is the difference between Cc and Bcc?

Answer: Everyone can see the people in Cc. People in Bcc are hidden from the other recipients.

slides.title: Attaching a File
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Click “Compose” and write an email.
  2. Step 2: Click the paperclip icon (“Attach files”).
  3. Step 3: Choose a file from “My Files 2025” (e.g., “My Letter”).
  4. Step 4: Click “Send.”
⭐ Activity: Attach a document to an email.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Click Compose. Fill in To and Subject.
  2. Click the paperclip icon at the bottom of the message window (Attach files).
  3. A window opens. Go to your folder, for example My Files 2025. Use the left side to move around.
  4. Click the file once, for example My Letter, then click Open.
  5. Type a short message that says what the file is.
  6. Wait until the file name shows at the bottom of the message, then click Send.

You should see the file name and its size. Wrong file? Click the small X beside its name. You can also drag a file from File Explorer into the message.

Power-user layer
  • Hold Ctrl and click several files to attach them together.
  • Gmail limits attachment size. For very large files, Gmail offers to share a Google Drive link instead.
  • Name files clearly, like CV_Jane_Wanjiru.docx, not Document1.
  • For a CV, save as PDF first (Word: File, Save As, choose PDF). The layout stays the same on any device.
  • Gmail may remind you if you write "attached" but forget the file. Always check the file name is shown before sending.
  • Never open attachments you did not expect.
Check yourself: How can you check that a file is attached before you press Send?

Answer: The file name (with its size) is listed at the bottom of the message window.

slides.title: Replying to an Email
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Open an email in your inbox.
  2. Step 2: Click “Reply” at the bottom.
  3. Step 3: Type your response (e.g., “Thanks for your message!”).
  4. Step 4: Click “Send.”
⭐ Activity: Reply to an email you receive.
Step-by-step layer
  1. In the Inbox, click the message to open it.
  2. Scroll to the bottom and click Reply. The curved arrow at the top-right of the message does the same.
  3. Notice that the sender's address is already in To and the subject starts with "Re:".
  4. Click in the box and type your answer.
  5. Click Send.

You should see your reply under the original message, in the same conversation. Common slip: clicking Reply all by mistake. That sends your answer to everyone on the message. Use plain Reply unless everyone needs to see it. Forward sends the message on to a new person.

Power-user layer
  • With shortcuts switched on, r replies and a replies to all.
  • Before using Reply all, look at who is in To and Cc.
  • Keep the same subject. That keeps the whole conversation in one thread.
  • Answer within a day or two, even if only to say "Received, I will reply on Friday".
  • Be short, polite and clear.
  • Before forwarding, scroll down. Old messages below may contain private information.
Check yourself: When should you use Reply all instead of Reply?

Answer: Only when everyone on the original message needs to read your answer. Otherwise reply to the sender only.

slides.title: Organizing Your Inbox
slides.content:
1. Delete: Remove unwanted emails (click trash icon).
  2. Archive: Hide emails without deleting (click archive icon).
  3. Folders/Labels: Group emails (e.g., “Family” or “Work”).
⭐ Activity: Delete an email from your inbox.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Tick the small box on the left of an email in the list.
  2. Delete: click the trash icon. The message goes to the Bin (called Trash in some versions).
  3. Archive: select an email and click the archive icon (a box with a down arrow). It leaves the Inbox but is kept safely.
  4. Label: select an email, click the label (tag) icon, choose Create new, type Family, and click Create.
  5. Look at the left list. Your new label is there. Click it to see its emails.

Deleted by mistake? Click Undo at once at the bottom-left. Later, open Bin, select the message and choose Move to inbox.

Power-user layer
  • Archive more, delete less. Archived mail still shows up when you search.
  • With shortcuts on, e archives, # (Shift+3) deletes and l opens labels.
  • Handle each email once: reply, archive or delete.
  • Use Unsubscribe on newsletters you never read, and Report spam for junk.
  • Tick several boxes to move many emails at once.
  • Bin is emptied after a while, so do not use it as storage.
Check yourself: What is the difference between archiving and deleting an email?

Answer: Archiving removes it from the Inbox but keeps it, and you can still search for it. Deleting moves it to the Bin, where it is later removed.

slides.title: Checking Your Work
slides.content:
1. Check: Did your email send? Check “Sent” folder.
  2. Sign Out: Click your profile picture → “Sign out.”
  3. Sign In: Reopen Gmail, enter email and password.
⭐ Activity: Sign in and out of Gmail.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Click Sent in the left list.
  2. Your newest email is at the top. Check the To address and subject.
  3. Click it to see the message and any attachment.
  4. To sign out, click your round profile picture at the top-right and choose Sign out.
  5. To sign in, go to gmail.com, type your email address, click Next, type your password, click Next.

You should see your Inbox again. Wrong password message? Check that Caps Lock is off. Click the eye icon to see what you typed. If you forgot it, click Forgot password? and follow the steps.

Power-user layer
  • Always sign out on shared or cyber café computers, then close the browser.
  • Closing the tab alone does not sign you out.
  • If Chrome asks to save the password on a shared computer, choose Never.
  • Not in Sent? Check Drafts. Maybe the message never went.
  • At the bottom-right of Gmail, "Last account activity" with Details shows recent sign-ins. Unknown places mean you should change your password.
Check yourself: You clicked Send but cannot find the message in Sent. Where else should you look?

Answer: Check Drafts, because it may not have been sent. Also check you are signed in to the correct account.

slides.title: Practical Activity
slides.content:
1. Task 1: Create a Gmail account (or sign in).
  2. Task 2: Send an email with a subject and 2 sentences.
  3. Task 3: Attach a file (e.g., “My Letter” from Week 2).
  4. Task 4: Reply to an email from the instructor.
✅ Checklist: Complete each task and celebrate progress!
Step-by-step layer
  1. Go to gmail.com. Create an account (Create account, For my personal use) or sign in.
  2. Click Compose. In To type a classmate's address. Subject: Hello from and your name. Write two sentences. Send.
  3. Compose again. Click the paperclip, choose My Letter from My Files 2025, wait for the file name to show, and Send.
  4. Open the instructor's email. Click Reply, type a thank-you, Send.
  5. Open Sent and check both emails are there.

Expected result: two sent emails, one with a paperclip, and a reply under the instructor's message. Stretch challenge: make a signature (Settings gear, See all settings, General, Signature) with your name and phone number.

Power-user layer
  • A good email has a greeting, one clear purpose, thanks and your name.
  • Before every Send, ask four questions: right person, clear subject, file attached, polite tone.
  • Practise by emailing yourself with an attachment. You learn without risk.
  • Use Ctrl+Enter to send.
  • Keep important documents also in a folder on your computer, not only in email.
Check yourself: Task: send yourself an email with a subject and an attachment. How do you know it worked?

Answer: It arrives in your Inbox with a paperclip icon beside it, and a copy is in Sent.

slides.title: Why This Matters
slides.content:
1. Send messages to friends or family.
  2. Share documents (e.g., letters, lists).
  3. Prepare for internet safety next week!
⏳ Note: Email is useful in daily life.
Step-by-step layer

Use email to earn and save this week.

  1. Write three real tasks you could do by email: send a CV, send a price quotation to a customer, send an invoice or school form.
  2. Create a professional address if you do not have one.
  3. Open your CV in Word. Click File, Save As, and choose PDF as the type. Save.
  4. Email the PDF to yourself with the subject CV - Your Name.
  5. Open the email in the Inbox and click the attachment to check it opens.

You should see your CV open from the email. If the file will not attach, check you saved it and look in the right folder.

Power-user layer
  • Many employers ask for applications by email, and customers expect quotations and invoices by email.
  • Use a subject like "Application: Sales Assistant - Jane Wanjiru". It helps the reader find you.
  • Many services send password resets to your email. If someone enters your inbox, they can enter your other accounts. Protect it.
  • Email gives a written record of what was agreed.
  • Reply quickly. Fast, polite replies build trust with clients.
Check yourself: Give two ways email can help you earn or save money.

Answer: For example, send your CV to employers, send quotations or invoices to customers, or avoid travel costs by sending documents instead of delivering them.

slides.title: Q&A and Homework
slides.content:
1. Ask: Any questions about Gmail?
  2. Homework:
    1. Send an email to a friend or family member.
    2. Attach a file to an email.
    3. Reply to an email or check your inbox.
  3. Next Week: Using the internet safely!
❓ Encourage: Ask questions and use handouts for practice.
Step-by-step layer

Common beginner questions:

  1. Is Gmail free? Yes, a basic personal account is free. You only need internet.
  2. I forgot my password. On the sign-in page click Forgot password and follow the steps. A recovery phone or email helps.
  3. I sent it to the wrong person. Click Undo straight away if you still see it. If not, send a short polite message asking them to delete it.
  4. My friend did not get my mail. Check Sent and the address spelling. Ask them to look in Spam.

Homework tip: ask your friend to reply so you practise both ways.

Power-user layer
  • Do the homework on a real address. Real replies teach more than practice mail.
  • Check your inbox once a day, at the same time.
  • Keep a notebook with your address and password in a safe place.
  • Write your questions down when you get stuck and bring them to class.
  • Little and often beats one long session.
Check yourself: Your friend says your email never arrived. Name two things you should check.

Answer: Check Sent to confirm it went and that the address was spelled correctly. Also ask your friend to look in their Spam folder.

slides.title: Internet and Online Safety
slides.content:
1. Objective: Learn to use the internet and stay safe.
  2. Today: Browse with Google Chrome and avoid scams.
  3. Why It Matters: Find information and protect yourself!
  4. What do you want to find online? (e.g., a recipe)
Step-by-step layer
  1. Check you are online. Click the Wi-Fi icon at the bottom-right of the taskbar. Choose your network and type the password if asked.
  2. Open Google Chrome.
  3. Write in your notebook one question you want answered online, such as a recipe or a weather forecast.
  4. On a clean page, write the heading "Safety rules". You will add to it during this lesson.

You should see Chrome open with a search box in the middle. Common slip: Wi-Fi connected but no internet. Turn the router off and on, or switch on a phone hotspot and join it from the Wi-Fi list.

Power-user layer
  • This module has two skills: finding things, and protecting yourself.
  • Pause before you click, type a password or pay. Scammers depend on hurry and excitement.
  • Treat the internet like a busy public market. Do not share anything you would not say out loud there.
  • Keep Windows updated. Updates fix security holes.
  • If something feels too good to be true, it probably is.
Check yourself: What are the two main skills in this module?

Answer: Finding information with a browser, and staying safe online.

slides.title: What Is the Internet?
slides.content:
1. A global network to find information and connect.
  2. Examples: Search for news, recipes, or weather.
  3. We’ll use Google Chrome, a web browser.
🌐 Explain: The internet is a digital library; show Chrome.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Open Chrome.
  2. Click the address bar, type weather today and press Enter.
  3. Look at the results. The answer comes from computers far away called servers.
  4. Click one result. Look at the address at the top. That is the website.
  5. Click the Back arrow to return to the results.

Remember three words. The internet is the worldwide network. A website is a set of pages on it. A browser is the program that opens them. Common slip: "No internet" message. Check Wi-Fi or your data bundle.

Power-user layer
  • Wi-Fi is not the internet. Wi-Fi only connects your computer to a router, and the router connects to the internet.
  • Videos and big downloads use far more data bundle than text pages.
  • Close tabs you do not need.
  • Not everything online is true. Check who wrote it, when, and whether a second trusted source agrees.
  • Official organisations and well-known news sites are usually better sources than anonymous posts.
Check yourself: Is Google the same as the internet?

Answer: No. Google is a search engine, one website that helps you find pages. Chrome is the browser that opens them.

slides.title: Opening Google Chrome
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Click Start (Windows icon, bottom-left).
  2. Step 2: Type “Chrome” in the search bar.
  3. Step 3: Click Google Chrome to open.
⭐ Activity: Open Chrome on your own computer.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Click Start (Windows icon at the bottom-left), or press the Windows key.
  2. Type Chrome. Do not press anything else yet.
  3. Click Google Chrome in the results, or press Enter.
  4. Wait a few seconds. A window opens.

You should see a search box and a long address bar at the top. Common slips:

  • Chrome is not found. Windows already has Microsoft Edge. It works almost the same.
  • The window is small. Double-click the title bar at the top, or click the square button next to the X.
Power-user layer
  • Right-click Chrome in the Start results and choose Pin to taskbar. Next time, one click opens it.
  • Alt+Tab switches between open programs.
  • Ctrl+N opens a new Chrome window.
  • The three dots at the top-right open Chrome's menu. Under Help, About Google Chrome, you can check for updates.
  • Browsers need updates to stay safe. Restart Chrome when it asks.
Check yourself: If Chrome is not installed, which browser is already on Windows?

Answer: Microsoft Edge.

slides.title: Understanding a Web Browser
slides.content:
1. Address Bar: Type website names (e.g., www.google.com).
  2. Tabs: Open multiple websites at once.
  3. Back/Forward Buttons: Navigate between pages.
⭐ Activity: Find and name the address bar and tabs in your browser.
Step-by-step layer
  1. Open Chrome.
  2. Address bar: the long box at the top. Click it, type a website name and press Enter.
  3. Tabs: the strip along the very top. Click the plus (+) to open a new tab and type another website.
  4. Click each tab to switch. Click the small X on a tab to close it.
  5. Back and Forward: arrows at the top-left. Beside them is the Reload button (circular arrow).
  6. Click the three dots at the top-right to see the menu.

You should be able to point to each part. If you closed a tab by mistake, press Ctrl+Shift+T to bring it back.

Power-user layer
KeysWhat it does
Ctrl+TNew tab
Ctrl+WClose tab
Ctrl+TabNext tab
Ctrl+Shift+TReopen closed tab
Ctrl+LGo to address bar
Alt+LeftBack
F5Reload

Do not keep dozens of tabs open. It slows the computer. Bookmark pages instead.
