⏳ Note: Cloud storage helps in real life.
Step-by-step layer

Cloud storage means your work is safe if a laptop is stolen or breaks. Practise protecting one important file:

  1. Upload your certificate scan to a folder "Documents".
  2. Check that it opens from your phone.
  3. Turn on two-step verification: myaccount.google.com, then Security.

You should see "2-Step Verification: On". Common slip: losing the phone used for verification; save backup codes in a safe place.

Power-user layer

Cloud storage supports remote teamwork: shared folders, comments and version history replace emailing files back and forth, which creates confusion about which is the latest. Treat Drive like a filing cabinet with a lock: tidy, named, and only shared with intended people. Back up the most valuable files in a second place. Next week: PDFs, which are ideal to send final documents.

Check yourself: Give one reason cloud storage is better than emailing attachments back and forth.

Answer: There is a single up-to-date file that everyone opens, so you avoid confusion over versions and can restore older versions.

slides.title: Q&A and Homework
slides.content:
1. Ask: Any questions about Google Drive?
  2. Homework:
    1. Upload 2 files to Google Drive.
    2. Create a folder and move a file into it.
    3. Share a file with someone via email.
  3. Next Week: Working with PDFs!
❓ Encourage: Ask questions and use handouts for practice.
Step-by-step layer

Likely questions:

  • Is Drive free? A Google account includes free space; check the current amount on Google's site.
  • Can others see my files? Not unless you share them or use "Anyone with the link".
  • I deleted a file by mistake. Open Trash on the left, right-click it and Restore.
  • Homework steps: upload 2 files; create folder; move a file; share with Viewer access; confirm they can open it.
Power-user layer

Homework tips: name your files properly before upload. After sharing, ask the person to confirm they can open it, and check Share to see they appear. Try removing access afterwards to learn how. Keep a note of which account you used. If you hit trouble, write down the exact message. Over time, learn to scan documents with the Drive mobile app and to search by file type.

Check yourself: You deleted a file in Drive today. Can you still get it back, and how?

Answer: Usually yes: open Trash, right-click the file and choose Restore, as long as it has not been permanently deleted or removed after the Trash period.

slides.title: Working with PDFs
slides.content:
1. Objective: Learn to view and annotate PDFs.
  2. Today: Use Adobe Acrobat Reader to manage documents.
  3. Why It Matters: Read and mark up files like forms or recipes!
  4. What PDFs have you seen? (e.g., a bill or form)
Step-by-step layer

A PDF is a document frozen in its final look. Try this to see the difference from Word.

  1. Open any Word file, then choose File, Save As, and pick PDF.
  2. Open the PDF by double-clicking it.
  3. Try to change a sentence. Most PDF viewers will not let you.

You should see the same fonts, pictures and page breaks on every phone or computer. That is the whole point of the format. Common slip: expecting the free Reader to rewrite text. Reader is for viewing, highlighting, commenting and filling forms. To change the words, go back to the Word original and export again.

Power-user layer

Keep the Word or Excel original. A PDF is the copy you send, not the file you work in. Name versions clearly, such as Budget_Jan.docx and Budget_Jan.pdf. Scanned PDFs are only pictures of paper, so you cannot select their text. Be careful with PDFs from strangers: do not enter M-Pesa PINs or ID numbers into a PDF form unless you trust who sent it. Next, learn how to fill and sign forms.

Check yourself: Name one document you would send as a PDF rather than a Word file, and why.

Answer: Anything that must look the same for the reader, such as a fee statement, CV or invoice. A PDF keeps the layout fixed and is harder to change by accident.

slides.title: What Is a PDF?
slides.content:
1. A file format for documents that look the same everywhere.
  2. Examples: Recipes, forms, manuals.
  3. Use Adobe Acrobat Reader (free) to open and edit.
📄 Explain: PDFs are “fixed” documents; show Acrobat Reader.
Step-by-step layer

Think of a PDF as a printout that lives on your screen: layout locked, easy to share, hard to edit. The first thing to learn is to recognise one.

  1. Open File Explorer and go to your Downloads folder.
  2. Look for files ending in .pdf. Click View, then tick File name extensions if you cannot see the ending.
  3. Check the icon. It usually shows the viewer app that opens it.

Typical Kenyan PDFs: KRA acknowledgement receipts, school fee structures, bank statements, payslips, and manuals. If a file will not open, the slip is often an incomplete download. Delete it and download again.

Power-user layer

Reader is free, but the word edit on the slide means mark up, not rewrite. Browsers like Edge and Chrome open PDFs too, so you are never stuck without a viewer. Some PDFs are protected with a password. Opening them needs the password from the sender, so ask instead of trying to guess. Pro habit: when a PDF has important numbers, keep a copy of the source spreadsheet too, since you cannot easily recalculate inside a PDF.

Check yourself: Why are PDFs good for sending a CV to an employer?

Answer: They look identical on any device, so fonts and layout do not break, and the reader cannot change your text by accident.

slides.title: Opening Adobe Acrobat Reader
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Click Start (Windows icon, bottom-left).
  2. Step 2: Type “Adobe Acrobat” in the search bar.
  3. Step 3: Click Adobe Acrobat Reader to open.
🖱️ Demo: Show how to open Acrobat; ensure it’s installed.
Step-by-step layer

You will open Reader many times, so make it quick.

  1. Click Start (or press the Windows key).
  2. Type Acrobat. Do not press Enter yet.
  3. When Adobe Acrobat Reader appears at the top, click it.

You should see a window with a menu bar (File, Edit, View) and a Home screen listing recent files. If nothing appears when you search, it is not installed. Download Reader from Adobe's official site only, and decline any extra offered software. Slip to avoid: opening the wrong program. Search results show Edge and Word too, so read the name.

Free option: right-click a PDF, choose Open with, and pick Microsoft Edge.

Power-user layer

Pin Reader to the taskbar: right-click its icon while open, then Pin to taskbar. Faster still, skip Reader entirely and double-click the PDF itself, because Windows opens it with the default viewer. Check Home, then Recent, to find files you worked on yesterday. If Reader asks to sign in, you can usually close that prompt and keep reading. Keep it updated: fake PDF readers are a common way for malware to spread, so install from the official source only.

Check yourself: What is the quickest way to open any PDF, without searching for Reader first?

Answer: Double-click the PDF file in File Explorer. Windows opens it with the default PDF viewer.

slides.title: Opening a PDF
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Open File Explorer, go to “My Files 2025.”
  2. Step 2: Double-click a PDF file (e.g., “Recipe.pdf”).
  3. Alternative: In Acrobat, click File → Open, select file.
📂 Practice: Open a sample PDF for practice.
Step-by-step layer

Let us open the file two ways and compare.

  1. Open File Explorer and click the folder where your file lives (the slide uses My Files 2025).
  2. Double-click Recipe.pdf. The page opens.
  3. Now close it. Open Reader, press Ctrl+O, pick the file, and click Open.

You should see the first page, with the file name on the tab at the top. Common slip: you cannot find the file because you saved it somewhere else. Use the search box in File Explorer and type part of the name, or check Downloads.

Power-user layer

Drag a PDF from File Explorer straight into an open Reader window and it opens. Use right-click, then Open with, when a different program grabs PDFs. In Reader, Recent files on the Home screen is often quicker than browsing. Keep a consistent folder system so you never lose files. A name like 2025-03_School_Fees.pdf sorts neatly and is easy to search. If a PDF opens blank, the file may be damaged: ask the sender to send it again.

Check yourself: You double-click a PDF and nothing happens. Name two things to try.

Answer: Right-click it, choose Open with, and pick Reader or Edge. If that fails, the file may be damaged, so download or request it again.

slides.title: Navigating a PDF
slides.content:
1. Scroll: Use mouse wheel or sidebar to move up/down.
  2. Zoom: Click View → Zoom In/Out.
  3. Page Navigation: Use arrows to change pages.
🧭 Show: Navigation in a multi-page PDF.
Step-by-step layer

Long PDFs, like a 40-page fee booklet, need quick movement.

  1. Scroll with the mouse wheel, or drag the scroll bar.
  2. Press Ctrl and + to zoom in, Ctrl and - to zoom out. Or use the zoom box in the toolbar.
  3. Type a page number in the page box at the top and press Enter to jump there.
  4. Press Ctrl+F and type a word, such as deadline, to search.

You should see the matching words highlighted. Common slip: zooming in so far that you think the text vanished. Choose Fit Page to reset.

Power-user layer

Experts rarely scroll. They search with Ctrl+F, use the thumbnail panel for pictures, and use bookmarks if the author made them. Ctrl+Home and Ctrl+End jump to the first and last page. On a phone, pinch to zoom. Scanned PDFs cannot be searched, because they are only images. If Ctrl+F finds nothing in a document you know contains the word, suspect a scan rather than a bug.

Check yourself: How do you find every mention of the word total in a 30-page PDF without reading it all?

Answer: Press Ctrl+F, type total, and press Enter to step through each match.

slides.title: Highlighting Text
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Open a PDF in Acrobat Reader.
  2. Step 2: Click the Highlight tool (marker icon).
  3. Step 3: Drag over text to highlight (e.g., a recipe step).
🖍️ Practice: Highlight a sample PDF.
Step-by-step layer

Highlighting helps you mark deadlines in a school circular or ingredients in a recipe.

  1. Open the PDF in Reader.
  2. Choose the Highlight tool. In the free Reader it is in the Comment toolbar or a floating bar after selecting text.
  3. Drag across the words. They turn yellow.
  4. Press Esc to stop highlighting.

Right-click a highlight to change its colour or delete it. Common slip: nothing highlights because the PDF is a scan (a picture). Then use a drawing or sticky note tool instead.

Power-user layer

Use colours with meaning: yellow for key facts, green for tasks, pink for questions. Do not highlight whole pages, as that defeats the purpose. Highlights are saved only when you save the file, so remember to Save afterwards. If you plan to send it, think about whether the other person should see your private notes; save a separate copy first. Edge and Chrome can also highlight PDFs if Reader is not installed.

Check yourself: Your highlights vanished after you closed the PDF. What probably went wrong?

Answer: You did not save the file after marking it. Highlights only stay if you save (File, Save or Save As).

slides.title: Adding Comments
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Click the Comment tool (speech bubble icon).
  2. Step 2: Click where you want to add a note.
  3. Step 3: Type your comment (e.g., “Try this recipe!”).
💬 Demo: Add a comment to a PDF.
Step-by-step layer

A comment is a sticky note on the page.

  1. Open the PDF and choose the Comment tool (speech bubble), or Add a comment in the toolbar.
  2. Click the spot where the note belongs.
  3. Type, for example, Check price with supplier.
  4. Click elsewhere to close it.

You should see a small bubble icon. Hover over it or double-click to read it again. The Comments list on the right shows every note. Common slip: typing a comment with no note selected. Click exactly where you want the bubble first.

Power-user layer

Write comments that can be acted on: say what to change, not just that something is wrong. Use Reply to answer someone else's comment, which keeps a conversation in one place. When a comment is done, mark it resolved or delete it. Remember comments travel with the PDF, so remove embarrassing or private ones before forwarding. In a group, ask people to use their own name in the author settings so you know who said what.

Check yourself: Why should you read comments before forwarding a PDF to a client?

Answer: Comments are saved inside the file, so private or unfinished notes would be seen by the client.

slides.title: Saving an Edited PDF
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Click File → Save As.
  2. Step 2: Choose “My Files 2025” folder.
  3. Step 3: Name file (e.g., “Recipe_Edited.pdf”).
💾 Practice: Save an edited PDF.
Step-by-step layer

Saving a copy protects the original.

  1. Click File, then Save As (or press Ctrl+Shift+S).
  2. Choose the folder, for example My Files 2025.
  3. Type a new name such as Recipe_Edited.pdf.
  4. Click Save.

You should see the new name in the title bar. Check in File Explorer that both files exist. Common slip: pressing Save and overwriting the original with your notes. Always use Save As when you want to keep a clean copy.

Power-user layer

Pick a naming rule and stick to it: Name_Topic_v2.pdf. Avoid names like final_final2.pdf. Saved annotations can be removed later only inside the full paid editor, so keep a clean original just in case. If the Save As window shows Save as type, make sure it says PDF. For a sensitive file, save it to a folder only you can reach, not a shared computer's Desktop. Next learn Print to PDF to produce files from any program.

Check yourself: What is the difference between Save and Save As, and which protects the original?

Answer: Save overwrites the current file. Save As makes a new copy under a new name, so it protects the original.

slides.title: Emailing a PDF
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Open Gmail (from Week 4).
  2. Step 2: Click Compose, attach PDF from “My Files 2025.”
  3. Step 3: Add recipient and subject, click Send.
📧 Practice: Email a PDF file.
Step-by-step layer

Sending a PDF by email is the daily workhorse of office life.

  1. Open Gmail and click Compose.
  2. Click the paperclip icon, then choose your PDF from the folder.
  3. Wait until the file name shows under the message box. That means it has finished uploading.
  4. Fill in To and Subject, type a short note, and click Send.

Common slip: pressing Send before the upload finishes, or attaching the wrong version. Read the file name under the message before sending.

Power-user layer

Mention the attachment in the body (Attached: Recipe_Edited.pdf), as that also helps you remember to attach it. Very big files may be refused by email; then upload to Drive and send a link instead. Do not email files containing ID numbers or bank details unless you must, and only to the right person. Double-check the recipient address, since one wrong letter sends your document to a stranger. Use a clear subject, like Fee statement - Term 2.

Check yourself: Your PDF is too large to attach. What is the usual alternative?

Answer: Upload it to Google Drive and email a view-only link instead of the file.

slides.title: Practical Activity
slides.content:
1. Task 1: Open a sample PDF in Acrobat Reader.
  2. Task 2: Highlight a sentence and add a comment.
  3. Task 3: Save as “Edited_PDF” in “My Files 2025.”
  4. Task 4: Email the PDF to the instructor.
✅ Checklist: Complete each task and celebrate progress!
Step-by-step layer

Worked answer for the four tasks.

  1. Open a sample PDF: double-click it, or open Reader and press Ctrl+O.
  2. Select the Highlight tool, drag over a sentence, then use Add a comment and click beside it. Type a short note.
  3. File, Save As, folder My Files 2025, name Edited_PDF.pdf, Save.
  4. Gmail, Compose, attach Edited_PDF.pdf, enter the instructor's address, subject Edited PDF - your name, Send.

Check: the sent email shows a paperclip and file name. Stretch challenge: add a second comment in another colour and email it to yourself, then open it to confirm your marks travelled.

Power-user layer

Experts finish by testing. After sending, open the file from the Sent folder to confirm what the reader sees. Time yourself: can you do all four tasks in under ten minutes? Speed comes from shortcuts: Ctrl+O, Ctrl+Shift+S, Ctrl+F. Write your own checklist for the steps you forget. When something fails, change one thing at a time, so you can learn which fix worked.

Check yourself: After Task 3, which two files should exist, and why does that matter?

Answer: The original PDF and Edited_PDF.pdf. Keeping both means a mistake in your edits cannot destroy the original.

slides.title: Why This Matters
slides.content:
1. View forms, recipes, or manuals.
  2. Add notes to important documents.
  3. Prepare for combining documents next week!
⏳ Note: PDF skills help in real life.
Step-by-step layer

Why spend a week on PDFs? Practise with real documents from your life.

  1. Pick a PDF you really need: a school circular, a payslip, or a manual.
  2. Highlight the one date or amount that matters.
  3. Add a comment saying what to do about it, such as Pay by 30th.
  4. Save a copy with the date in the name.

Now you have a document that reminds you. Common slip: marking too much. If everything is highlighted, nothing stands out.

Power-user layer

Professionals use PDFs for contracts, quotations, and reports because they look the same on every screen. The habit that separates experts is version control: keep the original, mark up a copy, and name both clearly. Soon you will merge a chart from Excel and text from Word into one report, then export it as PDF. Every skill this week is a link in that chain.

Check yourself: Give one real situation where highlighting and commenting on a PDF saves you time.

Answer: For example, marking a deadline and an amount in a fee circular with a note to pay, so you do not miss it later.

slides.title: Q&A and Homework
slides.content:
1. Ask: Any questions about PDFs?
  2. Homework:
    1. Open and highlight a PDF.
    2. Add a comment and save the file.
    3. Email the edited PDF to a friend.
  3. Next Week: Combining documents and spreadsheets!
❓ Encourage: Ask questions and use handouts for practice.
Step-by-step layer

Answers to common questions.

  • Can I edit the words in a PDF? Not in the free Reader. Change the Word file and export again.
  • Why can I not highlight? The PDF may be a scan, which is only a picture.
  • Where did my file go? Check the folder in the Save As window, or search File Explorer by name.
  • How do I make it smaller? Ask the sender for a smaller version, or send a Drive link.

Homework worked example: open, highlight, comment, Save As Name_Edited.pdf, attach in Gmail, send to a friend.

Power-user layer

Do homework in the same order the slide lists it, and confirm each step by checking the result. Ask your friend to tell you whether they could see the highlight and comment. If not, the file was probably not saved before attaching. Keep your questions specific: say what you clicked, what you expected, and what happened. That habit makes it easy for anyone to help you, now and at work.

Check yourself: You emailed an edited PDF, but your friend sees no highlight. What do you check first?

Answer: Whether you saved the PDF after highlighting and attached the saved copy, not the original.

slides.title: Document and Spreadsheet Integration
slides.content:
1. Objective: Create reports with text and data.
  2. Today: Use Word, Excel, and Google Drive together.
  3. Why It Matters: Make clear reports (e.g., budgets, plans)!
  4. What kind of report would you make? (e.g., a budget)
Step-by-step layer

Our goal: a one-page report with a table and chart. Plan before you click.

  1. Write the title: Monthly Budget, March.
  2. List three items and costs, for example Rent KES 8,000, Food KES 5,000, Transport KES 2,000.
  3. Decide who will read it: yourself, a chama, or a loan officer.

Tools: Excel for numbers, Word for words, Drive for sharing. Common slip: starting in Word and typing numbers by hand. Do the maths in Excel so a total is never wrong.

Power-user layer

Experts separate data from presentation. The numbers live in Excel, where they can be recalculated, and the report in Word explains them. Think about the reader first: a chama treasurer wants totals; a lender wants income and expenses side by side. Free option: LibreOffice Calc and Writer, or Google Sheets and Docs, work the same way. Next you will learn how to carry a chart across.

Check yourself: Which tool should hold the numbers, and which should hold the explanation?

Answer: Excel holds and calculates the numbers. Word holds the explanation and presents the chart.

slides.title: Why Combine Tools?
slides.content:
1. Word: Write professional reports or letters.
  2. Excel: Organize and visualize data (e.g., charts).
  3. Google Drive: Store and share your work.
🗂️ Recap: Week 2 (Word), Week 6 (Excel), Week 9 (Drive).
Step-by-step layer

Each tool does one job well.

  • Excel: calculates. Example: =SUM(B2:B4) adds your costs.
  • Word: explains. Example: a paragraph stating what the chart shows.
  • Drive: stores and shares from any phone.

Try it: a small shop owner tracks daily sales in Excel, writes a weekly summary in Word, and shares it with a partner through Drive. Common slip: pasting numbers into Word as plain text, which will not update. Keep the working version in Excel.

Power-user layer

Pro habit: one source of truth. If you change a price, change it in Excel, then refresh the chart and paste it again. Otherwise your report disagrees with your sheet. Name files so the pair stays obvious: Budget.xlsx and Budget_Report.docx. Be careful sharing files that include customer names or phone numbers; share only the summary. Later you can link Excel to Word so updates flow automatically, but pasting a picture is a fine start.

Check yourself: Why keep the working numbers in Excel instead of typing them into Word?

Answer: Excel recalculates totals and charts when numbers change, so the report cannot silently contain wrong sums.

slides.title: Reviewing Word and Excel
slides.content:
1. Word: Type and format text (Week 2).
  2. Excel: Use formulas and charts (Weeks 3, 6).
  3. Open: Start → Type “Word” or “Excel” → Click.
🖱️ Demo: Open both programs and review basics.
Step-by-step layer

Warm up before combining.

  1. Start, type Word, press Enter. Type a title and make it bold with Ctrl+B.
  2. Open Excel the same way. Type a label in A1 and a number in B1.
  3. Switch programs with Alt+Tab.

You should see two windows, which you can flip between. Common slip: saving to different places. Pick one folder for the whole project, so files are easy to find. Free equivalents: LibreOffice Writer and Calc, or Google Docs and Sheets.

Power-user layer

Useful shortcuts: Ctrl+S saves, Ctrl+Z undoes, Ctrl+B bolds, Alt+Tab switches window, Ctrl+Home returns to the top. Save early and often, and especially before pasting something big. If you are unsure what a button does, hover over it and read the tip. Expert users rely on a few shortcuts each day, not hundreds. Pick two and use them until automatic.

Check yourself: What shortcut lets you jump between open Word and Excel windows?

Answer: Alt+Tab.

slides.title: Creating a Data Table in Excel
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Open Excel, label A1:B1 as “Item,” “Cost.”
  2. Step 2: Enter data (e.g., “Food,” $50; “Travel,” $30).
  3. Step 3: Use SUM for total (e.g., B3: =SUM(B1:B2)).
📊 Practice: Create a table in Excel.
Step-by-step layer

Build the table correctly. The slide's total formula needs one careful look.

  1. In A1 type Item, in B1 type Cost.
  2. A2 Food, B2 50. A3 Travel, B3 30. Add more rows if you wish.
  3. In A4 type Total. In B4 type =SUM(B2:B3) and press Enter.

You should see 80. The total goes below the data, and the range covers only the numbers. A formula such as =SUM(B1:B2) in cell B3 would miss the Travel row and count itself, which Excel flags as a circular reference. Common slip: forgetting the equals sign.

Power-user layer

Click B4 and press Alt+= for AutoSum, which guesses the range. Check the highlighted range before pressing Enter. Format costs as currency: select B2:B4, Home, then Number format. If you add a new row inside the range, the total updates; if you add it below the total, it does not. Use Format as Table (Ctrl+T) when data will grow. Google Sheets uses the same =SUM formula.

Check yourself: Data is in B2:B5. Which cell and formula give the total?

Answer: Put it in B6, below the data, as =SUM(B2:B5).

slides.title: Creating a Chart in Excel
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Highlight table (e.g., A1:B2).
  2. Step 2: Click Insert → Column Chart.
  3. Step 3: Add title (e.g., “Monthly Budget”).
📈 Practice: Create a chart in Excel.
Step-by-step layer

A chart turns your table into a picture.

  1. Select A1:B3 (labels and numbers, not the Total row).
  2. Click Insert, then the Column chart icon, then Clustered Column.
  3. Click the chart title, delete the default text, and type Monthly Budget.

You should see one column per item, with height showing cost. Common slip: including the Total row, which makes one giant column that dwarfs the rest. Select only the items. Add axis titles with the plus button next to the chart.

Power-user layer

Choose the chart for the question. Compare items: columns. Parts of a whole: pie, only with few slices. Change over time: line. Remove clutter such as heavy gridlines, and label the units, for example KES. Make sure the axis starts at zero for columns, or the differences will look bigger than they are. Click the chart and use Chart Design to pick a clean style. Google Sheets: Insert, Chart.

Check yourself: Why should the Total row be left out of the selected chart range?

Answer: The total is much bigger than each item, so it would dominate the chart and squash the individual columns.

slides.title: Copying a Chart to Word
slides.content:
1. Step 1: In Excel, right-click chart → Copy.
  2. Step 2: Open Word, click where you want the chart.
  3. Step 3: Press Ctrl+V to paste.
📋 Demo: Copy and paste a chart into Word.
Step-by-step layer

Moving the picture across.

  1. In Excel, click the chart border and press Ctrl+C.
  2. Switch to Word, click where it should appear.
  3. Press Ctrl+V.
  4. Use the small Paste Options button that appears and choose Picture for a fixed image.

You should see the chart sitting in your text. Drag a corner handle to resize it. Common slip: pasting into the wrong place, such as mid-sentence. Press Enter first to create an empty line, then paste.

Power-user layer

Paste options matter. Keep Source Formatting and Embed carries the data with it; Picture creates a lightweight image that cannot change. Linked options update when the Excel file changes, but break if the file is moved. For reports you will email, Picture is safest and keeps file size down. Add a caption: right-click the chart, Insert Caption. Resize by corner handles to keep proportions.

Check yourself: You pasted a chart and it does not change when Excel numbers change. Why?

Answer: It was pasted as a picture or embedded copy, not linked. Update the chart and paste again.

slides.title: Writing a Report in Word
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Open Word, type a title (e.g., “Budget Report”).
  2. Step 2: Add text (e.g., “This shows my expenses.”).
  3. Step 3: Paste Excel chart below text.
  4. Step 4: Format (Bold title, 16pt).
📝 Guide: Write a short report in Word.
Step-by-step layer

A short report has structure.

  1. Type the title: Budget Report, March. Select it, choose the Title style from Home.
  2. Write two sentences: This report shows my monthly spending. Rent is the largest cost at KES 8,000.
  3. Press Enter, paste the chart.
  4. Under it, add a one-line conclusion.

You should see a title, text, and chart on one page. Common slip: formatting by hand every time. Use styles in the Home tab; they stay consistent and save time.

Power-user layer

Good reports answer three questions: what is this, what does it show, and what should the reader do? Put the key finding in words, not just the chart. Check the spelling with F7. Keep pages clean: a consistent font, one or two sizes. Read it aloud once; mistakes jump out. Before sending, check that the numbers in the text match the chart. Google Docs works the same way using Insert, Chart from Sheets.

Check yourself: Besides the chart, what is the one sentence every short report needs?

Answer: A plain-language finding, such as which cost is largest, so the reader does not have to guess from the picture.

slides.title: Saving Your Report
slides.content:
1. Step 1: In Word, click File → Save As.
  2. Step 2: Choose “My Files 2025” folder.
  3. Step 3: Name file (e.g., “My Report”).
💾 Practice: Save your report in Word.
Step-by-step layer

Name and place your report so you can find it.

  1. Click File, then Save As, then Browse.
  2. Choose your folder (My Files 2025).
  3. Type My_Report_March. Leave the type as Word Document.
  4. Click Save.

You should see the name in the title bar. Common slip: saving to a random default folder like Documents, then forgetting where it went. Look at the folder path in the Save window before pressing Save.

Power-user layer

Press Ctrl+S early and often. Turn on AutoSave if the file is on OneDrive, but a locally saved file needs manual saving. Avoid special characters in names. Add the date so versions are clear. Back up important files to Drive or a flash disk, since a computer can fail. Do not save work on a shared cyber cafe computer without deleting it afterwards, as others may open it.

Check yourself: Where would you look first if you cannot find the report you just saved?

Answer: In File Explorer, search the file name, or check Recent files in Word's File, Open list.

slides.title: Uploading to Google Drive
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Open Google Drive (drive.google.com).
  2. Step 2: Click “New” → “File upload.”
  3. Step 3: Select “My Report” from “My Files 2025.”
  4. Step 4: Share with view-only access (Week 9).
🌐 Practice: Upload and share your report.
Step-by-step layer

Putting the report online.

  1. Go to drive.google.com and sign in.
  2. Click New, then File upload.
  3. Pick the file and click Open. Wait for the upload message.
  4. Right-click the file, choose Share, then General access, then Anyone with the link, role Viewer.
  5. Click Copy link.

You should see the file in My Drive. Common slip: sharing as Editor, which lets others change your report. Set Viewer unless you want edits.

Power-user layer

Restricted sharing is safest: add individual email addresses rather than opening it to anyone with the link. Check who has access from the Share window later and remove people if needed. Do not share files containing customer data or ID numbers. A Word file uploaded to Drive stays a Word file; open with Google Docs to view in the browser. Organise with folders, as the capstone will require.

Check yourself: Which sharing role should you choose if people should read but not change your report?

Answer: Viewer.

slides.title: Practical Activity
slides.content:
1. Task 1: Create an Excel table with 3 items and costs.
  2. Task 2: Add a SUM formula and a column chart.
  3. Task 3: Create a Word report with text and pasted chart.
  4. Task 4: Save and upload to Google Drive.
✅ Checklist: Complete each task and celebrate progress!
Step-by-step layer

Full worked answer.

  1. Excel: A1 Item, B1 Cost. Rows: Food 5,000; Transport 2,000; Airtime 500. A5 Total, B5 =SUM(B2:B4). It shows 7,500.
  2. Select A1:B4, Insert, Column chart. Title it Weekly Costs.
  3. Copy the chart and paste into Word under a title and two sentences.
  4. Save as Report.docx.
  5. Upload to Drive, set Viewer sharing.

Check: the chart shows three columns and the total is correct. Stretch: add a fourth item and see the total and chart change.

Power-user layer

When tasks fail, find which link broke: number, chart, paste, save, or upload. Test with a second person: can they open your link? Time the task, then repeat from memory without the slide. If a formula gives an odd answer, click the cell and check the range. Notice how each step handed output to the next; that is how every office workflow is built.

Check yourself: Your total shows 5,500 instead of 7,500. What do you check?

Answer: Click the total cell and check that the SUM range covers every cost row, and that all costs are numbers, not text.

slides.title: Why This Matters
slides.content:
1. Create clear reports with data.
  2. Share plans or budgets easily.
  3. Prepare for the capstone project next week!
⏳ Note: Integration skills help in real life.
Step-by-step layer

Where does this show up?

  1. A boutique owner prepares a monthly sales summary for a loan application.
  2. A chama treasurer sends contributions and a chart to members.
  3. A student submits a project with a data table and graph.

All three use the same chain: Excel, Word, then share. Try it with your own real figures this week: even five lines of household spending is good practice. Common slip: waiting for a perfect example. Start small.

Power-user layer

Reports build trust. Accurate numbers, tidy layout, and a clear sentence of conclusion tell the reader you are careful. The same chain scales: later you may use pivot tables and Power BI instead of simple charts. The thinking stays constant: collect data, calculate, show, explain, share. Next week the capstone asks you to repeat it, plus slides and Zoom.

Check yourself: Name the three-step chain used in this module for turning data into a shared report.

Answer: Excel for numbers and chart, Word for the report, Drive for sharing.

slides.title: Q&A and Homework
slides.content:
1. Ask: Any questions about Word, Excel, or Drive?
  2. Homework:
    1. Create a report with an Excel chart.
    2. Save and upload to Google Drive.
    3. Share with a friend via email.
  3. Next Week: Capstone project!
❓ Encourage: Ask questions and use handouts for practice.
Step-by-step layer

Common questions.

  • Can I use Google Sheets and Docs instead? Yes. Insert, Chart in Sheets, then Edit, Copy, and paste into Docs.
  • Why is my chart blank? You probably selected cells without numbers. Reselect labels and numbers.
  • Where did my upload go? Check My Drive, or search by name.
  • Who can see my file? Only people you shared with, or anyone with the link if you chose that.

Homework: report with chart, upload, share a view-only link by email.

Power-user layer

Use the homework to rehearse the capstone. Do it without the slides, then check yourself against them. If you share a link by email, test it yourself in a private window to see what the recipient sees. Write down one thing that confused you and bring it. Good learners track their stumbling blocks, because those are what the next lesson should fix.

Check yourself: You shared a link but your friend says Access denied. What setting do you fix?

Answer: Change General access from Restricted to Anyone with the link, or add their email address, with Viewer role.

slides.title: Artificial Intelligence – Your New Digital Assistant
slides.content:
1. Learn how AI can save you time, help you make better decisions, and open new opportunities.
💡 Reflection: Have you ever heard of AI before? What do you think it does?
Write down your thoughts or say them aloud.
Step-by-step layer

AI is software that learns patterns from large amounts of examples and uses them to answer or predict. Do this short reflection.

  1. Write down: what do I think AI does?
  2. List two apps you use that suggest or predict things.
  3. Revisit your answer at the end of the module.

You will probably notice you already meet AI daily. Common slip: thinking AI is a robot. Most AI is just software on your phone or the web.

Power-user layer

Beginners often swing between fear and hype. A balanced view: AI is a powerful tool that is sometimes wrong. Keep a notebook of what you try and how well it worked. Check what is currently available, because tools change often, and judge each one by your tasks, not by its marketing. Never put private customer data or passwords into a public AI tool.

Check yourself: In your own words, is AI a robot or software? Give an example.

Answer: Mostly software, such as spelling suggestions or video recommendations on your phone.

slides.title: What is AI?
slides.content:
1. AI means machines that can learn and make decisions.
  2. It uses data to find patterns and give smart answers.
  3. It’s not magic — it’s math + logic + examples.
🔍 Analogy: AI is like a smart student who learns from past papers and helps you solve new questions.
Step-by-step layer

Think of AI as a student who has studied many past papers. Show it enough examples and it spots patterns.

  1. Take 3 M-Pesa messages and notice that normal ones look alike.
  2. An odd one, such as a huge amount at night, stands out.
  3. An AI trained on many examples learns that difference and flags the odd one.

That is pattern spotting. Common slip: believing AI understands like a person. It predicts what fits the pattern, which is why it can sound confident and still be wrong.

Power-user layer

Learn two ideas: training (learning from examples) and prediction (using what it learned). Good data in, good results out. If the examples are biased or old, answers will be too. Chat assistants predict likely words, so they can invent facts, called hallucinations. Always ask for sources and verify important facts yourself. You do not need maths to use AI well, but you do need a questioning mind.

Check yourself: Why can an AI sound confident and still be wrong?

Answer: It predicts what fits patterns from its training, rather than knowing facts, so it can produce plausible but false answers.

slides.title: Why Should You Care?
slides.content:
1. AI helps you do tasks faster.
  2. It gives better results than guessing.
  3. It can help you earn more or save more.
🤔 Think: What’s one task you do often that takes time? Imagine AI doing it for you.
Step-by-step layer

Make this concrete by finding a time sink.

  1. List tasks you repeat weekly, such as replying to customers or making posters.
  2. Mark the ones that take longest.
  3. Pick one and write: Draft a polite M-Pesa payment reminder for a customer who owes KES 1,500.
  4. Try it in an AI assistant and edit the result.

You should get a usable draft in seconds. Common slip: sending it unchecked. Always read and personalise.

Power-user layer

AI saves time on first drafts, summaries and ideas. It does not replace your judgment. Measure benefit honestly: did it really save time after you corrected it? Do not claim AI will make you earn more; it helps only if you apply it well. Do not paste private customer details into public tools. Use placeholders like Customer A instead.

Check yourself: Name one task you repeat that AI could help draft, and what you would still check yourself.

Answer: For example, customer messages. I would check names, amounts and tone before sending.

slides.title: AI You Already Use Daily
slides.content:
1. M-Pesa: fraud alerts, transaction summaries.
  2. YouTube/TikTok: video suggestions.
  3. Google Translate: instant language help.
  4. Facebook: friend suggestions, auto-tagging photos.
📱 Quick Poll: Have you used any of these today? Think about which ones you use most often.
Step-by-step layer

You use AI more than you think. Do a quick audit.

  1. Open M-Pesa messages. Notice fraud warnings and transaction summaries.
  2. Open YouTube or TikTok. The home feed is chosen for you from what you watched.
  3. Try Google Translate on a Swahili sentence.
  4. Write which apps you used today.

You should see a list of at least three. Common slip: assuming recommendations are neutral. They are built to keep you watching, so notice how much time you spend.

Power-user layer

Spotting AI in daily life makes you a smarter user. Ask: what data does this app collect about me? Review privacy settings on your phone and apps. Remember recommendations reflect your past clicks, so they can narrow what you see. Translation tools help but can miss slang and local context, so check important messages with a fluent speaker. Fraud alerts help, yet never share your M-Pesa PIN with anyone.

Check yourself: Why does your video feed show different videos from your friend's?

Answer: The app learns from what each person watches and recommends similar content, so feeds differ.

slides.title: AI for Small Business
slides.content:
1. Track sales trends automatically.
  2. Predict which products will sell more.
  3. Manage stock levels.
  4. Send targeted messages to customers.
🏪 Local Example: Imagine your shop knows which items will run out next week — that’s AI helping.
Step-by-step layer

Shop owners can apply simple AI-style thinking even in Excel.

  1. Record daily sales of three items in columns for four weeks.
  2. Add =AVERAGE(B2:B8) for each week.
  3. If sugar sells 20 packets a week and stock is 30, you will run out in about a week and a half. Reorder.

Specialised AI tools automate this and spot trends, but they need clean records first. Common slip: expecting AI to predict from messy or missing data.

Power-user layer

The best preparation is good records. Without recording sales, no tool can forecast. Start with a simple sheet, then consider tools later. Check what is currently available and whether it fits dukas and small shops. Keep customer phone numbers private, and ask permission before sending marketing messages. Judge any tool by one question: does it help me make a better decision this week?

Check yourself: What must a shop have before any AI tool can predict its sales?

Answer: Consistent, accurate records of past sales and stock.

slides.title: AI for Personal Productivity
slides.content:
1. Voice-to-text: speak instead of typing.
  2. Smart typing: auto-complete messages.
  3. Calendar suggestions: best time to meet.
  4. Photo sorting: group by faces or places.
🎤 Try It: Use voice-to-text on your phone. Do you ever struggle with typing long messages?
Step-by-step layer

Try these four on your phone.

  1. Open Messages or Notes and tap the microphone on the keyboard. Say a short sentence in English or Swahili.
  2. Type half a message and see the suggestions.
  3. Open your Calendar and add an event to see time suggestions.
  4. Search your photo app for a place or a person.

You should see words appear as you speak. Common slip: speaking too fast or in a noisy place. Speak clearly, then correct errors by hand.

Power-user layer

Voice typing is excellent for long messages, but always proofread numbers and names, since those are errors that cost money. Auto-complete can change a word you meant, so reread before sending. Photo sorting uses face data, so check your privacy settings. Productivity comes from small habits: pick one feature, use it daily for a week, then decide whether to keep it.

Check yourself: What must you proofread most carefully after using voice-to-text?

Answer: Names and numbers, such as amounts and phone numbers, because they are the most costly mistakes.

slides.title: AI for Learning
slides.content:
1. Chatbots that explain topics in simple words.
  2. AI quizzes that adjust to your level.
  3. Apps that correct your pronunciation.
  4. Study summaries from long notes.
🧑‍💻 Demo: Ask ChatGPT or Bing Copilot a basic question. See how it answers!
Step-by-step layer

Use an AI chatbot as a patient tutor.

  1. Write: Explain what a spreadsheet formula is in simple words, with one example using KES.
  2. Read the answer.
  3. Follow up: Now give me 3 practice questions.
  4. Answer them, then ask it to mark your work.

Then check one fact in your notes or a trusted source. Common slip: letting it do the work. Learning happens when you try first.

Power-user layer

Use AI to explain, quiz and summarise, not to do your assignments for you. Ask it to explain at your level and to tell you when it is unsure. Verify facts, especially health, law and money. Check what is currently available, as free tools and limits change. Your own notes and teacher stay the main source. Teach the idea back in your own words to see if you truly understand it.

Check yourself: How can you use AI to learn rather than to cheat?

Answer: Try the question yourself first, then ask it to explain, quiz you and check your answers.

slides.title: AI for Data Analysis
slides.content:
1. Automatically creates charts from data.
  2. Spots patterns you might miss.
  3. Writes summaries and recommendations.
  4. Saves hours of manual work.
📊 Showcase: See a sample Excel sheet, then an AI-generated chart and insight.
Step-by-step layer

AI can describe data, but you must verify it.

  1. Make a small table: Month, Sales for Jan to Apr, with made-up numbers.
  2. Ask an assistant: Here is sample sales data. What trend do you see and what chart suits it?
  3. Check its claim with your own chart or formula, such as =(D2-B2)/B2.

Common slip: pasting real customer or patient data into a public tool. Use sample or anonymised figures only. Never upload names or ID numbers.

Power-user layer

AI can misread columns or miscalculate. Treat its output as a suggestion and recompute key figures in Excel. Describe your question clearly: who is the audience, what decision is needed. Anonymise data first. In professional work, check your organisation's rules before using any online tool with operational data. Learn Excel basics well; they let you check what AI tells you.

Check yourself: Why should you recompute an AI's numbers in Excel?

Answer: AI can make arithmetic or reading mistakes, so important figures must be verified independently.

slides.title: Free AI Tools You Can Try Today
slides.content:
1. ChatGPT / Bing Copilot: Ask questions, get answers.
  2. Canva Magic Design: Create posters and graphics.
  3. Google Lens: Identify objects, translate signs.
  4. Grammarly: Improve your writing.
🌐 Explore: Try one of these tools after class and share your experience next time!
Step-by-step layer

Pick one tool and try one small task. Check what is currently available, since free offers change.

  1. Choose a chat assistant. Sign in only if needed.
  2. Type: Write a 3-line poster text for a shop selling second-hand clothes in Nairobi.
  3. Edit the result.
  4. Try Google Lens on a printed sign in another language.

Common slip: believing every free tool is safe. Read what data it keeps, and never enter passwords or ID details.

Power-user layer

Compare tools by task, not fame. Keep a list: tool, task, result, worth keeping? Free versions may limit use or change. Do not install unknown apps from links in messages. Use official stores. Remember that Grammarly and similar tools read your text, so avoid private documents. Using two tools on the same task teaches you their differences quickly.

Check yourself: What should you never type into a free AI tool?

Answer: Passwords, ID numbers, PINs, and private customer or patient details.

slides.title: How to Start Using AI
slides.content:
1. Pick one task you do often.
  2. Search for an AI tool that helps with it.
  3. Try it with small, safe data.
  4. Keep what works, drop what doesn’t.
📝 Example: Typing long messages? Use voice-to-text. Making posters? Try Canva.
Step-by-step layer

A four-step trial.

  1. Choose one task, such as writing messages.
  2. Find a tool and try it with sample text.
  3. Rate the result 1 to 5 and note what you fixed.
  4. Repeat three times, then decide to keep or drop.

Example: ask for a polite reminder that rent is due on the 5th. Compare with your own version. Common slip: judging after one try. Run it several times with different wording.

Power-user layer

Start with low-risk tasks: drafts, ideas, summaries. Increase trust slowly. Use fake data when testing. A habit that pays off is saving your best prompts in a note, so you can reuse them. If a tool never saves you time after fixes, drop it without guilt. Check what is currently available now and again, since better options appear.

Check yourself: Why test a tool several times before deciding?

Answer: One result may be lucky or unlucky. Several tries show how consistent it is.

slides.title: Skills to Work Well with AI
slides.content:
1. Ask clear questions (called prompts).
  2. Check AI’s answers — don’t trust blindly.
  3. Combine AI help with your own thinking.
💬 Prompt Practice: Good: “Give me 3 tips to grow a small shop in Kenya.” Bad: “Tell me about business.”
Step-by-step layer

A prompt is your instruction. Good prompts include role, task, audience and format.

  1. Weak: Tell me about business.
  2. Better: You are a small business coach in Kenya. Give me 3 low-cost ways to attract customers to a mama mboga stall. Use short bullet points.
  3. Read the answer, then follow up: Make tip 2 more specific.

Then verify: does each tip fit your area and budget? Common slip: accepting the first answer.

Power-user layer

Three core habits: be specific, iterate, verify. Give context but not secrets. Ask the AI to show its steps or sources, then check them. If the answer is vague, your prompt probably was. Combine AI with your own thinking: you know your customers, it does not. Keep a library of prompts that worked. Critical reading is the real skill.

Check yourself: Rewrite this weak prompt: Help me with my shop.

Answer: Example: Give me 3 ways to reduce unsold stock in my small clothes shop in Eldoret, in bullet points.

slides.title: Risks & How to Stay Safe
slides.content:
1. Don’t share private info (ID, passwords).
  2. Double-check facts — AI can be wrong.
  3. Don’t copy blindly — learn and improve.
  4. Keep learning — AI changes fast.
⚠️ Remember: AI is a helper, not a master. You’re still in control.
Step-by-step layer

Safety checklist before pressing Send.

  1. Does the text contain a name, ID number, phone number, PIN or password? Remove it.
  2. Is the answer a fact that matters (money, health, law)? Verify elsewhere.
  3. Did you copy it word for word? Rewrite it in your voice.

Example: instead of pasting a customer list, write Customer A owes KES 2,000. Common slip: trusting a confident answer. Scammers also use AI voices and messages, so confirm unexpected money requests by calling the person on a known number.

Power-user layer

Risks include wrong answers, privacy leaks, bias, over-dependence and scams. Protect yourself: strong unique passwords, no secret details in public tools, and a pause before acting on urgent messages. Schools and employers may have rules about AI use, so follow them and be honest about when you used it. Remember: you are responsible for what you send or submit, not the tool.

Check yourself: What is the safe way to ask an AI about a customer's debt?

Answer: Replace names and numbers with placeholders such as Customer A, and never share ID or phone details.

slides.title: Call to Action
slides.content:
1. Try one AI tool this week.
  2. Use it for one task (typing, learning, designing).
  3. Share your experience in the next class.
✅ Homework: Pick one tool, use it, and tell us what happened!
Step-by-step layer

Make your call to action concrete.

  1. Write the tool you will try.
  2. Write the task: for example, Create a short Swahili message to remind clients about Friday's appointment.
  3. Set a day and time, such as Saturday morning.
  4. After trying it, write three lines: what worked, what failed, what you changed.

You should come to class with a real experience. Common slip: planning but never trying. Do it in five minutes, today.

Power-user layer

Reflection makes the experience useful. When sharing, mention the exact prompt and what you corrected, because that teaches others. Listen to classmates' failures too; they save you time. Keep experimenting weekly with one new use. Check what is currently available instead of copying old advice. Remember to keep personal details out of what you share.

Check yourself: What three things should you report back after trying an AI tool?

Answer: What worked, what did not work, and what you had to correct.

slides.title: Bonus: AI in Kenya
slides.content:
1. Local banks use AI for fraud detection.
  2. Kenyan startups use AI for agriculture (predicting weather, crop diseases).
  3. AI chatbots help with customer service in local businesses.
🌍 Discussion: Where else could AI help in our country?
Step-by-step layer

Discuss local use cases and what could go wrong.

  1. Banks watch for unusual transactions and flag them.
  2. Farm tools can combine weather and crop pictures to suggest actions.
  3. Chatbots answer common customer questions.

Exercise: pick a local problem, such as long clinic queues. Write what data would be needed (appointment times, visit counts) and who would own that data. Common slip: forgetting privacy. Health and money data are very sensitive.

Power-user layer

Local context matters: languages like Swahili and sheng, patchy internet, and mobile-first users. Ask whether a tool works in your language and on a low-end phone. Good projects start with a real problem, not with the technology. Data protection matters; ask how data is stored and who sees it. Check what is currently available in Kenya instead of assuming.

Check yourself: Why might a chatbot built abroad struggle with Kenyan customers?

Answer: It may not understand Swahili, sheng or local context such as M-Pesa and place names.

slides.title: Bonus: The Future of AI
slides.content:
1. AI is getting better at understanding language and images.
  2. More jobs will use AI tools in the future.
  3. Learning AI basics now gives you an advantage.
🚀 Encouragement: You don’t need to be a programmer to use AI. Curiosity and practice are enough!
Step-by-step layer

Prepare for a changing future with small habits.

  1. Each month, try one new AI feature in a tool you already use.
  2. Write down what it did well and badly.
  3. Improve one basic skill AI cannot replace: clear writing, numbers or customer care.

Example: you use AI for a first draft, then add local details only you know. Common slip: believing predictions about jobs. Nobody knows exactly; stay adaptable instead.

Power-user layer

Stay curious, not anxious. Skills that last include spotting errors, asking good questions, communicating, and handling data responsibly. Follow reliable sources and test claims yourself. Be wary of get-rich-quick AI schemes. Learn Excel and basic data skills, since they help you check AI work. The advantage comes from consistent practice, not from owning a tool.

Check yourself: Name two skills that stay valuable even as AI improves.

Answer: For example, checking facts and communicating clearly with customers.

slides.title: Capstone Project and Review
slides.content:
1. Objective: Combine all skills for a final project.
  2. Today: Create, present, and share a report.
  3. Why It Matters: Use all tools in real life!
  4. What project would you like to create? (e.g., a budget)
Step-by-step layer

The capstone ties together everything. Plan it first.

  1. Choose your topic, such as a monthly household budget.
  2. List the 4 items and amounts, for example Rent 8,000; Food 5,000; Transport 2,000; Airtime 500.
  3. Sketch the outputs: Excel table and chart, Word report, PDF, 3 slides, Drive folder, email, Zoom talk.

Common slip: starting without a plan, then redoing work. Spend 5 minutes writing the plan on paper first.

Power-user layer

Experts plan backwards from the deliverable: who receives it, in what form? Break the work into steps and finish each before the next. Keep all files in one folder with clear names. Expect small problems, and solve them one at a time. A finished simple project beats an unfinished impressive one. Use sample data if your real figures are private.

Check yourself: Why write a plan before opening any software?

Answer: It shows the steps and files needed, so you avoid redoing work.

slides.title: What Is the Capstone Project?
slides.content:
1. Create a budget report (Word, Excel).
  2. Present it (PowerPoint, Zoom).
  3. Share it (Google Drive, Gmail, PDF).
  4. Use all tools from Weeks 1-11.
🛠️ Explain: The project is a real-world task.
Step-by-step layer

Your budget report is a real-world task.

  1. Excel holds the numbers and chart.
  2. Word explains them in a short report, then exports as PDF.
  3. PowerPoint gives a 3-slide summary.
  4. Drive stores everything in one folder.
  5. Gmail sends the link, and Zoom is where you present.

Check: at the end you will have an .xlsx, .docx, .pdf, .pptx, and a shared folder. Common slip: naming files carelessly. Use Budget_Report.pdf, not New1.pdf.

Power-user layer

Think like a client: the final package should be easy to open, read and trust. Use consistent numbers everywhere, since a total that differs between Excel and the slides ruins credibility. Check files on a different device or in Drive preview. If time is short, prioritise correctness over decoration. Free equivalents: Sheets, Docs, Slides, Google Meet.

Check yourself: List the final files you should have at the end of the capstone.

Answer: An Excel file, a Word report, its PDF, a PowerPoint file, plus a Drive folder shared with a link.

slides.title: Step 1 – Create an Excel Table
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Open Excel (Week 3, 6).
  2. Step 2: Label A1:B1 as “Item,” “Cost” (e.g., “Rent,” $500).
  3. Step 3: Enter 4 items; use SUM for total.
  4. Step 4: Create a column chart (Week 6).
📊 Practice: Create a budget table in Excel.
Step-by-step layer

Build the first piece.

  1. Open Excel. A1 Item, B1 Cost.
  2. Enter four items in A2:B5 (Rent 8000, Food 5000, Transport 2000, Airtime 500).
  3. In A6 type Total, in B6 type =SUM(B2:B5). You should see 15500.
  4. Select A1:B5 (not the total), Insert, Column chart. Add title Monthly Budget (KES).

The slide's total formula should sum the cost rows only. Common slip: including row 1, or the total itself, in the range. Save as Budget.xlsx.

Power-user layer

Sort items largest to smallest (Data, Sort) to make the chart readable. Add a percentage column: =B2/$B$6, formatted as percent, to show each item's share. The dollar signs lock the total cell when copied down. Format costs with thousands separators. Check that your total matches a calculator. Stretch: add a Savings row and see how the chart reacts.

Check yourself: Costs are in B2:B5. Write the total formula and say where it goes.

Answer: In B6, below the data, type =SUM(B2:B5).

slides.title: Step 2 – Write a Report in Word
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Open Word (Week 2).
  2. Step 2: Type title (e.g., “My Budget Report”).
  3. Step 3: Add text (e.g., “This shows my expenses.”).
  4. Step 4: Copy-paste Excel chart (Week 11).
📝 Guide: Write a report in Word.
Step-by-step layer

Write the report.

  1. Open Word and type My Budget Report. Apply the Title style.
  2. Write: This report shows my monthly expenses. Rent is the largest cost, KES 8,000 of KES 15,500.
  3. Go to Excel, copy the chart (Ctrl+C), return to Word and paste (Ctrl+V) below the text.
  4. Add a one-sentence conclusion and save as Budget_Report.docx.

Check the figures in your text match the chart. Common slip: the chart is pasted over text. Press Enter first to make a clean line.

Power-user layer

Use headings for structure: Summary, Details, Recommendation. Keep the chart close to the sentence about it. Give the chart a caption. Run spell check with F7. Read the page as the recipient: what question will they have? Answer it in a sentence. Insert page numbers if the report grows. Save often, and keep a backup copy in Drive.

Check yourself: What should you check after pasting the chart into Word?

Answer: That the numbers in your text match the chart, and that the chart sits on its own line and is sized to fit the page.

slides.title: Step 3 – Save as PDF
slides.content:
1. Step 1: In Word, click File → Save As.
  2. Step 2: Choose “PDF” format, save in “My Files 2025.”
  3. Step 3: Open in Acrobat Reader to check (Week 10).
📄 Practice: Save as PDF and check in Acrobat.
Step-by-step layer

Create the PDF.

  1. In Word, click File, then Save As, and choose the folder.
  2. In the type box choose PDF. Name it Budget_Report.pdf.
  3. Click Save. (File, Export, Create PDF also works.)
  4. Open the PDF in Reader and flip through each page.

You should see the same layout as Word. Common slip: the chart is cut across two pages. Go back to Word, resize or add a page break, then export again.

Power-user layer

Always inspect the PDF; do not assume it matches. Check page breaks, fonts and images. The PDF is final; fix errors in Word and export again. In the Save dialog, Options lets you choose which pages to export. A smaller file attaches to email more easily. LibreOffice and Google Docs also export to PDF through File, Download or Export. Keep the Word file for future edits.

Check yourself: After exporting, you spot a typo in the PDF. What is the right fix?

Answer: Correct it in the Word file and export a new PDF. Reader cannot rewrite the text.

slides.title: Step 4 – Create a Presentation
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Open PowerPoint (Week 7).
  2. Step 2: Create 3 slides (title, text, chart).
  3. Step 3: Apply a theme; add an image.
  4. Step 4: Save as “My Project” in “My Files 2025.”
📽️ Practice: Create slides for your project.
Step-by-step layer

Make three simple slides.

  1. Open PowerPoint and choose a blank presentation. Apply a theme from the Design tab.
  2. Slide 1: title My Monthly Budget and your name.
  3. Slide 2: three short bullets, for example the largest costs and total.
  4. Slide 3: paste the Excel chart (Ctrl+V).
  5. Save as My_Project.pptx.

Common slip: too much text. Aim for under six words per bullet, so people can read from afar.

Power-user layer

One idea per slide. Use large text (at least 24 point) and strong contrast. Add an image only when it helps. Rehearse aloud with the slide show: press F5. Use Esc to exit. Add a closing question or next step. Free equivalents: Google Slides or LibreOffice Impress. Remember to keep personal numbers private if you present to others.

Check yourself: Why should slide bullets be short?

Answer: The audience reads while listening. Short bullets are easy to scan and let you speak the details.

slides.title: Step 5 – Upload to Google Drive
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Open Google Drive (Week 9).
  2. Step 2: Upload Word, PDF, and PowerPoint files.
  3. Step 3: Create a folder “My Project 2025.”
☁️ Practice: Upload files to Drive.
Step-by-step layer

Put the project in one tidy place.

  1. Open drive.google.com. Click New, then New folder. Name it My Project 2025.
  2. Double-click the folder to open it.
  3. Click New, File upload, and select your Word, PDF and PowerPoint files (hold Ctrl to pick several).

You should see all three files listed. Common slip: uploading into the main My Drive instead of the folder. Open the folder before you upload.

Power-user layer

Folder-level sharing is efficient: share the folder once and everything inside is shared. Choose Viewer. Check files open in Drive preview. Uploading again with the same name may create a duplicate or a new version, so tidy up. Never leave sensitive files shared with Anyone with the link. Remove sharing when the purpose has ended.

Check yourself: What is the advantage of sharing a folder instead of each file?

Answer: One link or permission covers every file inside, so it is simpler and consistent.

slides.title: Step 6 – Share via Email
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Open Gmail (Week 4).
  2. Step 2: Compose email, attach PDF.
  3. Step 3: Share Google Drive link (view-only).
📧 Practice: Email your project files.
Step-by-step layer

Send it all professionally.

  1. In Drive, right-click the folder, Share, set Anyone with the link as Viewer, then Copy link.
  2. In Gmail, click Compose.
  3. Attach Budget_Report.pdf.
  4. Write: Hello, please find my budget report attached. The full project is here: then paste the link.
  5. Add the subject Budget Project - your name and Send.

Common slip: forgetting that the link is set to restricted, which shows Access denied. Test it first.

Power-user layer

Be courteous: greeting, purpose, sign-off. Keep the subject specific. Attach only what is needed, and give the link for the rest. Open your sent email and click the link to test. Double-check the recipient. Do not email private details unless necessary. A clear email shows professionalism, and good habits here carry into any workplace.

Check yourself: Why both attach the PDF and share a Drive link?

Answer: The PDF is readable immediately, and the link gives access to the full project without a large email.

slides.title: Step 7 – Present in Zoom
slides.content:
1. Step 1: Join a Zoom meeting (Week 8).
  2. Step 2: Share PowerPoint via Screen Share.
  3. Step 3: Present slides, explain report.
🎤 Practice: Present your project in Zoom.
Step-by-step layer

Present with confidence.

  1. Join the meeting from the link or ID (Week 8). Check mic and camera.
  2. Open your PowerPoint first, so it is ready.
  3. In Zoom, click Share Screen, choose the PowerPoint window, then Share.
  4. Start the slide show, speak to each slide for about a minute.
  5. Click Stop Share when done.

You should see a green frame around the shared window. Common slip: sharing the wrong window or the whole screen with private notifications. Close other apps first.

Power-user layer

Rehearse once before the call. Plan the order: what is it, key numbers, what you suggest. Look at the camera, not the slide. Mute when not speaking. If data bundles are limited, turn off video and keep the share on. Have the PDF ready as a backup. Free alternative: Google Meet also shares screens. Ask for questions at the end.

Check yourself: What should you do before sharing your screen to avoid showing private things?

Answer: Close other apps and windows, and share only the presentation window.

slides.title: Practical Activity
slides.content:
1. Task 1: Create Excel table and chart (4 items).
  2. Task 2: Write Word report with chart; save as PDF.
  3. Task 3: Create 3-slide PowerPoint.
  4. Task 4: Upload to Google Drive, share via Gmail, present in Zoom.
✅ Checklist: Complete each task and celebrate progress!
Step-by-step layer

Complete worked answer, in order.

  1. Excel: four items, =SUM(B2:B5), column chart.
  2. Word: title, two sentences, pasted chart. Save as PDF.
  3. PowerPoint: title, text and chart slides.
  4. Drive: folder, upload files, share Viewer. Gmail: PDF and link. Zoom: share screen and present for three minutes.

Self-check: do the totals match in the Excel, Word and slides? Can a friend open your link? Stretch challenge: record your Zoom talk and ask a friend for two improvement points.

Power-user layer

Experts do a final quality pass: numbers consistent, names clear, links tested, sensitive data removed. Time your talk. Note one thing to improve next time. A project you can finish end to end is an achievement; keep the files as a portfolio sample for your own records. Replace personal figures with sample data if you share them publicly.

Check yourself: Which three checks would you do before sending the project?

Answer: Check numbers match across files, test the Drive link, and remove any private information.

slides.title: Review of Skills
slides.content:
1. Week 1-2: Files, typing.
  2. Week 3-6: Spreadsheets, internet.
  3. Week 7-11: Presentations, Zoom, Drive, PDFs.
  4. Today: Combine all for real-world tasks!
🎉 Celebrate: Review all skills learned.
Step-by-step layer

Use this as a self-audit.

  1. Weeks 1 to 2: save, name and find a file; type with care.
  2. Weeks 3 to 6: build a table, use =SUM, make a chart, search the web safely.
  3. Weeks 7 to 11: slides, Zoom, Drive, Gmail, PDF.
  4. Rate each from 1 to 5. Practise the lowest one today for ten minutes.

Common slip: only practising what you already do well. Aim at your weakest skill.

Power-user layer

Skills fade without use. Spaced practice works: short sessions often beat one long one. Teach someone else; explaining shows gaps. Keep a log of skills and the date you last used them. Pick one skill beyond this course, such as pivot tables or Power Query. Fix mistakes by checking one step at a time. Confidence comes from repetition, not talent.

Check yourself: Which skill from this course are you least confident in, and what ten-minute practice will you do?

Answer: Answers vary. A good answer names one skill and one specific small task, such as building an Excel chart from five lines of spending.

slides.title: Why This Matters
slides.content:
1. Create reports, budgets, or plans.
  2. Share and present ideas confidently.
  3. Use computers for daily life!
⏳ Note: Capstone skills help in real life.
Step-by-step layer

Where will you use this? Write three real uses.

  1. A budget for your household or chama.
  2. A short report or CV sent as a PDF.
  3. A presentation to a group, shared by Drive and Zoom.

Then choose one and do it for real in the next week, using your own figures. You should end with a file you actually use. Common slip: keeping skills in class only. Link each new skill to a task from your life.

Power-user layer

Digital skills compound. Each tool you learn makes the next easier. Be proud of small wins and keep a folder of your best work. Build good habits of safe sharing, clear naming and checking your work. When you meet a new program, apply the same questions: what does it make, where does it save, how do I share it?

Check yourself: Name one real task in your life where you can use these skills this week.

Answer: Answers vary, for example a monthly budget report or a PDF CV.
